questions.subject: Accounting concepts & standards
questions.q: Under AS-1, which of the following is a fundamental accounting assumption?
o: Money measurement, dual aspect and conservatism
Prudence, materiality and substance over form

questions.subject: Final accounts
questions.q: A trader's capital on 1-4-2025 was Rs. 4,00,000. During the year he introduced Rs. 60,000 and withdrew Rs. 40,000. Profit for the year (before interest on capital) was Rs. 1,20,000. Interest on capital is 6% p.a. What is the closing capital?
questions.e: Interest on capital = 6% on Rs. 4,00,000 = Rs. 24,000. Closing capital = 4,00,000 + 60,000 - 40,000 + 1,20,000 - 24,000 = Rs. 5,16,000. Interest on capital is an appropriation, reducing divisible profit and hence closing capital.

questions.subject: Trial balance & errors
questions.q: Which error would NOT affect the agreement of the trial balance?
o: Omission of a complete transaction from the books
Recording a purchase in the sales book
Posting Rs. 5,000 instead of Rs. 500 to both debit and credit
Writing the wrong amount in both the debit and credit entries
questions.e: Complete omission leaves both debit and credit sides equally short, so totals still agree. Posting a wrong figure to only one side, or a one-sided error, would disturb agreement.

questions.subject: Depreciation
questions.q: A machine bought on 1-7-2024 for Rs. 2,40,000 (residual value Rs. 20,000, life 8 years) is depreciated on straight-line basis. What is depreciation for the year ended 31-3-2025?
questions.e: Annual SLM depreciation = (2,40,000 - 20,000)/8 = Rs. 27,500. Used for 9 months (Jul-Mar): 27,500 x 9/12 = Rs. 20,625. Depreciation is charged pro-rata for the period of use in the year of purchase.

questions.subject: Depreciation
questions.q: Under the diminishing balance method, depreciation is charged on:
o: The written-down (book) value at the beginning of the year
The revalued amount at year end
questions.e: In the written-down-value method, a fixed percentage is applied each year to the reducing book value, so the charge falls year by year. The straight-line method charges on original cost (less residual).

questions.subject: Bills of exchange
questions.q: A bill of exchange is drawn by A on B for Rs. 50,000 payable 3 months after date, dated 10-1-2026. What is its maturity date (2026 is not a leap year)?
questions.e: Three months after 10-1-2026 is 10-4-2026; three days of grace are added, giving 13-4-2026. Days of grace apply to time bills (not bills payable on demand).

questions.subject: Bills of exchange
questions.q: When a bill is dishonoured, the entry in the drawer's books for noting charges paid by the drawee is:
o: Debit Noting Charges account, credit Drawee
questions.e: Noting charges borne initially by the holder are ultimately recoverable from the drawee, so the drawer's entry debits the drawee's (personal) account and credits bank/cash. The drawee's liability increases by the noting charges.

questions.subject: Bank reconciliation
questions.q: In a bank reconciliation statement prepared from the cash book balance, a cheque issued but not presented is:
o: Deducted from the cash book balance
Added to the pass book balance
Added to the cash book balance
questions.e: A cheque issued but not yet presented has been recorded in the cash book but not in the pass book, so the cash book shows a lower balance; it is added back to the cash book balance to reach the pass book figure.

questions.subject: Consignment
questions.q: Goods sent on consignment are recorded by the consignor as:
o: An expense in the P&L account
Stock with the consignee (part of closing stock)
questions.e: Until sold by the consignee, goods on consignment remain the consignor's stock and unsold consignment stock is valued at cost plus proportionate non-recurring expenses. No sale is recorded on mere despatch.

questions.subject: Consignment
questions.q: In consignment accounts, 'del credere commission' is paid to the consignee for:
o: Selling goods above the invoice price
Bearing the risk of bad debts on credit sales
questions.e: Del credere commission is an extra commission compensating the consignee for guaranteeing collection from debtors, i.e., bearing bad-debt risk. Ordinary commission is for selling; over-riding commission rewards sales above invoice price.

questions.subject: Joint venture
questions.q: A and B enter a joint venture sharing profits 3:2. A supplies goods costing Rs. 60,000 and B incurs selling expenses of Rs. 6,000. Sales by B are Rs. 90,000. What is B's share of profit?
questions.e: Joint venture profit = 90,000 - 60,000 - 6,000 = Rs. 24,000. B's 2/5 share = Rs. 9,600. Each co-venturer's costs and the venture sales are combined in the memorandum joint venture account.

questions.subject: Partnership accounts
questions.q: Interest on drawings is charged by the firm to a partner. In the firm's books it is:
o: Debited to the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account
Credited to the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account
questions.e: Interest on drawings is a gain to the firm, so it is credited (income) to the P&L Appropriation Account, increasing divisible profit. Interest on capital is the corresponding charge, debited to the same account.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: A, B and C share profits 5:3:2. B retires and A and C take his share equally. What is the new profit-sharing ratio?
questions.e: B's 3/10 share is split equally: A gains 3/20 and C gains 3/20. New shares: A = 5/10+3/20 = 13/20; C = 2/10+3/20 = 7/20, i.e., 13:7. The gaining ratio here is 1:1.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: On admission of a partner, general reserve appearing in the old balance sheet is:
o: Credited to all partners including the new partner
Credited to the old partners' capital accounts in the old ratio
questions.e: Undistributed reserves belong to the partners who earned them, so the general reserve is distributed to old partners in the old profit-sharing ratio. The new partner has no claim on past reserves.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: A firm earned super profit of Rs. 30,000. Goodwill is valued at 3 years' purchase of super profit. What is the goodwill?
questions.e: Goodwill = super profit x number of years' purchase = 30,000 x 3 = Rs. 90,000. Super profit is average maintainable profit minus normal profit on capital employed.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: On dissolution, unrecorded assets realised are:
o: Credited to the Bank Account only
Debited to the partners' capital accounts
questions.e: Any amount realised from an unrecorded asset is a gain on realisation, credited to the Realisation Account. The corresponding debit is to Bank. Unrecorded liabilities paid are debited to Realisation Account.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: Realisation expenses of Rs. 8,000 are paid by partner X on behalf of the firm on dissolution. The firm's entry is:
o: Debit X's Capital Account, credit Realisation Account
Debit Realisation Account, credit X's Capital Account
questions.e: Expenses borne by a partner on the firm's behalf increase what the firm owes that partner: debit Realisation Account (dissolution loss/expense) and credit the partner's capital account.

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: A company forfeits 1,000 shares of Rs. 10 each (Rs. 8 called up) for non-payment of the first call of Rs. 3. Amount credited to Share Forfeiture Account is:
questions.e: Amount received = application + allotment = Rs. 8 - Rs. 3 = Rs. 5 per share, i.e., Rs. 5,000. Share Forfeiture Account is credited with what was actually received, not the called-up amount.

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: Forfeited shares are reissued at Rs. 9 per share (face value Rs. 10). The maximum discount allowed on reissue when Rs. 5 per share was forfeited is:
questions.e: Discount on reissue cannot exceed the amount forfeited per share (Rs. 5); a Rs. 1 discount is within the limit. The discount is debited to Share Forfeiture Account on reissue.

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: Securities premium received on issue of shares can be used for:
o: Writing off preliminary expenses and issuing fully paid bonus shares
Creating a general reserve for any purpose
questions.e: Section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013 restricts securities premium to specified uses: issuing bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses, buy-back premium, etc. It cannot be used for dividends.

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: Debentures issued as collateral security are shown in the balance sheet:
o: By a note below the loan, not as a separate liability
questions.e: Collateral debentures are a secondary security; only the primary loan appears as a liability, with a note disclosing the debentures held as collateral. Recording both would double-count the liability.

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: Interest on debentures is:
o: Credited to the debentureholders' capital accounts
A charge against profits, payable even if there are no profits
questions.e: Debenture interest is a contractual charge and must be paid irrespective of profits, unlike dividends which are an appropriation. It is debited to the P&L Account as a finance cost.

questions.subject: Accounting concepts & standards
questions.q: Closing stock is valued at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower. This follows:
questions.e: Anticipating losses but not profits is the prudence/conservatism convention, embodied in AS-2's lower-of-cost-or-NRV rule. It prevents overstatement of assets and profit.

questions.subject: Capital vs revenue
questions.q: Which of the following is a capital expenditure?
o: Annual repairs keeping a machine in working order
Cost of installing a new machine, including freight and erection
questions.e: Installation, freight and erection bring the asset to working condition and are capitalised as part of the machine's cost. Repairs maintaining existing capacity and routine operating costs are revenue expenditure.

questions.subject: Provisions
questions.q: A provision for doubtful debts is created @ 5% on debtors of Rs. 2,00,000. Additionally a specific provision of Rs. 6,000 is needed. Total provision is:
questions.e: General provision = 5% of 2,00,000 = Rs. 10,000 plus specific Rs. 6,000 = Rs. 16,000 total. AS-29 requires provisions for probable obligations; general provisions reflect expected credit losses on the portfolio.

questions.subject: Final accounts
questions.q: Goods costing Rs. 40,000 destroyed by fire; the insurer admits a claim of Rs. 30,000. The net loss debited to P&L is:
questions.e: Loss = cost 40,000 - claim admitted 30,000 = Rs. 10,000 debited to P&L. The claim admitted is credited to the goods destroyed account / recognised as insurance claim receivable.

questions.subject: Final accounts
questions.q: If gross profit is 25% on cost, the gross profit margin on sales is:
questions.e: GP 25% on cost means on cost 100, GP 25, sales 125; margin on sales = 25/125 = 20%. To convert mark-up to margin: 25/125. This conversion is tested frequently.

questions.subject: Rectification of errors
questions.q: A credit purchase of Rs. 12,000 was wrongly recorded in the sales book. The rectification entry is:
o: Debit Suspense Rs. 12,000, credit Purchases Rs. 12,000
Debit Purchases Rs. 12,000, credit Sales Rs. 12,000
Debit Sales Rs. 12,000 and Purchases Rs. 12,000; credit Debtors Rs. 12,000 and Creditors Rs. 12,000
questions.e: The wrong entry was Dr Debtor 12,000 / Cr Sales 12,000. Rectification reverses it (Dr Sales, Cr Debtor) and records the true purchase (Dr Purchases, Cr Creditor). Combined: debit Sales and Purchases 12,000 each; credit Debtor and Creditor 12,000 each.

questions.subject: Rectification of errors
questions.q: A trial balance shows total debits exceeding credits by Rs. 4,500. The difference is temporarily placed in:
questions.e: An unlocated difference is parked in a Suspense Account (debited here since debits exceed credits) until the error is found. It appears in the balance sheet and is closed once rectified.

questions.subject: Final accounts
questions.q: Sale of old machinery at book value involves:
o: No entry, being a non-cash item
questions.e: Sale at book value: the asset leaves the books (credit Machinery) and cash comes in (debit Bank). If sold above/below book value, the difference goes to P&L as profit/loss on sale.

questions.subject: Final accounts
questions.q: Outstanding wages of Rs. 15,000 appear in the trial balance. In final accounts they are shown:
o: In both trading account and balance sheet
Only in the balance sheet as a current liability
questions.e: Items already in the trial balance are shown only once. Since outstanding wages are already debited in the trial balance (expense recorded), only the liability side remains: current liability in the balance sheet.

questions.subject: Depreciation
questions.q: The primary objective of providing depreciation is:
o: Valuation of the asset at market price
Allocation of the depreciable cost over the asset's useful life
questions.e: Depreciation is a cost-allocation process under the matching concept, spreading depreciable amount over useful life. It is not a valuation exercise, though it incidentally builds no fund unless a sinking fund is created.

questions.subject: Inventories (AS-2)
questions.q: Under AS-2, inventories are valued at:
o: Lower of cost and net realisable value
questions.e: AS-2 (Valuation of Inventories) mandates lower of cost and NRV, applying prudence. Cost includes purchase cost, conversion cost and other costs to bring inventory to its present location and condition.

questions.subject: Provisions (AS-29)
questions.q: A contingent liability is:
o: Recognised as a liability in the balance sheet
Disclosed by note, not recognised, unless the outflow is remote
questions.e: AS-29: contingent liabilities are disclosed (not recognised) unless outflow is remote (then even disclosure is skipped). Only present obligations with probable outflow and reliable estimate are provided for.

questions.subject: Events after BS date (AS-4)
questions.q: An event occurring after the balance sheet date that requires adjustment is:
o: A fire destroying stock before the year-end but reported after
Issue of bonus shares after year-end
A flood destroying a factory after year-end
questions.e: AS-4: adjusting events evidence conditions existing at the balance sheet date. A fire before year-end (condition existed) is adjusting; dividend declarations and post-year-end floods are non-adjusting, merely disclosed.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: In the absence of a partnership agreement, profits are shared:
o: As decided by the senior partner
In the ratio of time devoted
questions.e: Section 13 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932: absent agreement, profits and losses are shared equally, no interest on capital or drawings is allowed, and no salary is payable to partners.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: In the absence of agreement, interest on a partner's loan to the firm is payable at:
questions.e: The Partnership Act, 1932 fixes 6% p.a. on partners' loans/advances absent agreement. Note this differs from interest on capital, which needs an express agreement.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: A new partner is admitted for a 1/4 share. Old partners A and B share 3:2. The sacrificing ratio is:
questions.e: With no information on how the new share is acquired, it is assumed the old partners sacrifice in the old ratio, 3:2. Sacrificing ratio = old ratio - new ratio; the assumption applies only when unspecified.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: X and Y share 2:1. Z is admitted for 1/6 share, acquired entirely from X. The new ratio is:
questions.e: X sacrifices 1/6: X's new share = 2/3 - 1/6 = 1/2; Y stays 1/3; Z gets 1/6. Ratio 1/2:1/3:1/6 = 3:2:1 on a common denominator of 6.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: On retirement, the retiring partner's share of goodwill is:
questions.e: Goodwill is raised/adjusted through continuing partners' capital accounts (debit, in gaining ratio) with the retiring partner's capital credited for his share. No goodwill account remains in the books under the common approach.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: A and B share equally. A dies; profits to the date of death are estimated at Rs. 60,000 for the full year and death occurs after 3 months. A's share of profit to death is:
questions.e: Pro-rata profit to death = 60,000 x 3/12 = Rs. 15,000; A's half = Rs. 7,500, credited to A's capital/executors account. Time-basis apportionment is used absent a better estimate.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: On dissolution, the Realisation Account is debited with:
o: Book value of assets transferred to it
questions.e: All assets (except cash/bank and fictitious assets) are transferred to Realisation Account at book value on the debit side; liabilities go to the credit side. Sale proceeds are credited; payments to creditors debited.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: A firm is dissolved; a creditor of Rs. 20,000 accepts stock of Rs. 18,000 in full settlement. The Realisation Account is:
questions.e: When a liability is settled by transferring an asset, Realisation Account is credited with the full book amount of the liability discharged (Rs. 20,000); the Rs. 2,000 difference is a gain on realisation. No bank entry passes.

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: Buy-back of equity shares out of free reserves requires creation of:
o: Capital Redemption Reserve equal to the nominal value bought back
questions.e: Section 69 of the Companies Act, 2013: on buy-back out of free reserves/securities premium, an amount equal to the nominal value of shares bought back is transferred to the Capital Redemption Reserve.

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: Right shares are offered to:
o: Existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings
questions.e: A rights issue is an offer to existing equity shareholders in proportion to paid-up capital held (Section 62). Renunciation of rights is permitted unless the articles forbid it.

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: Under the Companies Act, 2013, a private company must have a minimum paid-up capital of:
questions.e: The Companies (Amendment) Act, 2015 removed minimum paid-up capital requirements (earlier Rs. 1 lakh for private and Rs. 5 lakh for public companies). Verify against the current bare Act for exam day.

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: Calls in advance are shown in the balance sheet as:
o: A current liability under 'Other current liabilities'
questions.e: Calls received in advance are money received before due -- a liability (other current liabilities) until the call is made. Interest may be paid on calls in advance per the articles.

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: Loss on issue of debentures is written off:
o: In the year of issue fully
Over the life of the debentures
questions.e: Discount/loss on issue of debentures is a deferred charge amortised over the debenture term (matching concept). It appears as a non-current asset (unamortised) until written off.

questions.subject: Bills of exchange
questions.q: A promissory note differs from a bill of exchange mainly because:
o: It is a promise to pay, made by the debtor himself
questions.e: A promissory note contains an unconditional promise by the maker (debtor) to pay; a bill is an unconditional order by the drawer to the drawee. Notes need no acceptance and have two parties; both are negotiable.

questions.subject: Bills of exchange
questions.q: Accommodation bills are drawn:
o: To help a party raise funds temporarily, without trade consideration
questions.e: Accommodation bills lack consideration and are drawn mutually to accommodate a party's finance needs. On maturity the drawer remits funds to the drawee who honours the bill.

questions.subject: Bank reconciliation
questions.q: If the bank pass book shows a lower balance than the cash book, a possible cause is:
o: A direct deposit by a customer recorded in the cash book
Interest allowed by the bank and recorded in the cash book
A cheque issued but not presented for payment
Bank charges debited by the bank but not yet recorded in the cash book
questions.e: Bank charges reduce the pass book balance with no corresponding cash book entry yet, so the pass book reads lower. Unpresented cheques would instead make the cash book lower than the pass book.

questions.subject: Depreciation
questions.q: A change in depreciation method from WDV to SLM is treated as:
o: A change in accounting estimate, applied prospectively
A change in accounting policy with retrospective effect
questions.e: Per AS-6, a change in depreciation method is a change in accounting estimate (revising expected pattern of benefits), applied prospectively from the date of change. It is not a policy change requiring retrospective restatement.

questions.subject: Depreciation
questions.q: Machine cost Rs. 5,00,000, WDV depreciation @ 20% p.a. After 2 years the method changes to SLM with remaining life 6 years and no residual value. Depreciation in year 3 is:
questions.e: WDV after 2 years = 5,00,000 x 0.8 x 0.8 = Rs. 3,20,000. SLM over remaining 6 years = 3,20,000/6 = Rs. 53,333. The change applies prospectively on the carrying amount at the change date.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: Interest on capital is allowed only when:
o: There are profits in all cases
The partnership deed provides for it
questions.e: Interest on capital is an appropriation needing express agreement in the deed; the Partnership Act, 1932 allows none by default. It is payable only out of profits unless the deed says otherwise.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: A, B, C share 3:2:1. C is guaranteed a minimum profit of Rs. 30,000. Firm profit is Rs. 1,20,000. How much does B get?
questions.e: C's normal share = 1,20,000 x 1/6 = Rs. 20,000, short of the guarantee by Rs. 10,000, borne by A and B in 3:2: A bears 6,000, B bears 4,000. B gets 40,000 - 4,000 = Rs. 36,000.

questions.subject: Bills of exchange
questions.q: A bill for Rs. 30,000 is renewed: the drawee pays Rs. 10,000 cash and accepts a new bill for the balance plus interest @ 12% p.a. for 3 months. The new bill amount is:
questions.e: Balance = 30,000 - 10,000 = Rs. 20,000. Interest for 3 months @ 12% = 20,000 x 12% x 3/12 = Rs. 600. New bill = Rs. 20,600. Interest on renewal is debited to the drawee and added to the new bill.

questions.subject: Bills of exchange
questions.q: Under rebate on bills discounted, the rebate for the unexpired period is:
o: Carried forward as a liability (unearned discount)
questions.e: Discount earned on a discounted bill relates partly to the next period; the unexpired portion is carried forward as 'rebate on bills discounted' (a liability), following the accrual concept.

questions.subject: Average due date
questions.q: The average due date of two amounts Rs. 20,000 due in 2 months and Rs. 30,000 due in 5 months is (base date = today):
questions.e: Average due date = (20,000x2 + 30,000x5)/50,000 = (40,000+1,50,000)/50,000 = 3.8 months from base date. Amounts are weighted by their due periods.

questions.subject: Account current
questions.q: In an Account Current, interest is calculated on:
o: Each transaction at a flat rate
The products of balances and days
questions.e: Account Current uses the product method: each balance x days outstanding, interest = total products x rate/365. Red-ink interest handles negative/favourable balances.

questions.subject: Consignment
questions.q: Goods costing Rs. 25,000 are invoiced to the consignee at Rs. 30,000 (cost + 20%). The loading to be eliminated on unsold stock of Rs. 6,000 (invoice price) is:
questions.e: Loading = 20/120 of invoice price. On unsold stock of 6,000: 6,000 x 20/120 = Rs. 1,000, credited back via stock reserve. Unsold consignment stock must be stated at cost to the consignor.

questions.subject: Consignment
questions.q: Consignor's non-recurring expenses (freight, insurance in transit) on consignment are:
o: Added to the cost of goods for valuing unsold stock
questions.e: Non-recurring expenses incurred to bring goods to the consignee's godown add to cost; proportionate amounts attach to unsold stock. Recurring expenses (godown rent, selling) are period costs charged to the consignment account only.

questions.subject: Joint venture
questions.q: In a joint venture with separate books, the co-venturer's share of profit is transferred to:
o: His personal account with the venture
questions.e: With separate JV books, each co-venturer has a personal account; his profit share is credited there and remitted on settlement. The Joint Venture Account itself shows the venture's profit.

questions.subject: Incomplete records
questions.q: Incomplete records: opening capital Rs. 1,50,000, closing capital Rs. 2,10,000, drawings Rs. 30,000, fresh capital introduced Rs. 20,000. Profit for the year is:
questions.e: Profit = closing capital + drawings - opening capital - fresh capital = 2,10,000 + 30,000 - 1,50,000 - 20,000 = Rs. 70,000 (statement of affairs method). Drawings are added back, fresh capital deducted.

questions.subject: Final accounts
questions.q: A debtor pays Rs. 9,800 in full settlement of Rs. 10,000. Discount allowed is:
o: Rs. 200, debited to Discount Allowed Account
questions.e: Discount allowed = 10,000 - 9,800 = Rs. 200, an expense debited to Discount Allowed Account. Settlement discounts are financing-nature items, shown separately from trade discount (which is never recorded).

questions.subject: Final accounts
questions.q: Trade discount is:
o: Deducted from the invoice price and never recorded separately
questions.e: Trade discount is a price reduction netted in the invoice; only the net amount enters the books. Cash discount for prompt payment is recorded separately as discount allowed/received.

questions.subject: Final accounts
questions.q: Prepaid insurance of Rs. 12,000 for the year; 3 months relate to next year. Adjustment entry at year-end:
o: Debit Insurance Rs. 3,000, credit Prepaid Insurance
Debit Prepaid Insurance Rs. 3,000, credit Insurance Rs. 3,000
questions.e: 3 months' prepaid = 12,000 x 3/12 = Rs. 3,000 carried forward as an asset: debit Prepaid Insurance (asset), credit Insurance expense. The P&L bears only 9 months' cost.

questions.subject: Final accounts
questions.q: Rent received in advance Rs. 24,000 appears in the trial balance. It is shown:
o: Only on the liabilities side of the balance sheet
Only in the P&L credit side
Both in P&L and balance sheet
questions.e: Already recorded (trial balance), so only the unexpired portion's liability remains: shown once as a current liability. Double treatment applies only to adjustments outside the trial balance.

questions.subject: Final accounts
questions.q: A loan of Rs. 1,00,000 taken on 1-10-2025 @ 12% p.a.; books close 31-3-2026. Outstanding interest is:
questions.e: Interest for 6 months = 1,00,000 x 12% x 6/12 = Rs. 6,000, debited to P&L and shown as outstanding liability. Accrual concept requires recognising expense incurred though unpaid.

questions.subject: Final accounts
questions.q: Gross profit Rs. 80,000; carriage inwards Rs. 5,000 was wrongly debited to carriage outwards. Correct gross profit is:
questions.e: Carriage inwards belongs in the trading account (direct expense). Wrongly placed in P&L as carriage outwards, it understated gross profit by Rs. 5,000; correction raises GP to Rs. 85,000. Net profit is unchanged overall.

questions.subject: Cash flow basics
questions.q: Net profit Rs. 50,000 after charging depreciation Rs. 10,000 and writing off preliminary expenses Rs. 4,000. Which is added back for operating cash flow (indirect method)?
questions.e: Both are non-cash charges debited to P&L, added back to net profit under the indirect method. Depreciation is operating; preliminary expense write-off is also non-cash (amortisation).

questions.subject: Cash flow basics
questions.q: Sale of machinery (book value Rs. 40,000) for Rs. 46,000 is shown in the cash flow statement as:
questions.e: Full sale proceeds of a fixed asset are an investing cash inflow; the Rs. 6,000 profit is deducted from operating profit (indirect method) to avoid double counting. Classification follows the activity, not the gain.

questions.subject: Ratio analysis
questions.q: Which ratio measures long-term solvency?
questions.e: Debt-equity (long-term debt/equity) assesses long-term solvency and financial risk. Current ratio is short-term liquidity; turnover and GP ratios measure efficiency and profitability.

questions.subject: Ratio analysis
questions.q: Current assets Rs. 3,00,000 (including stock Rs. 80,000 and prepaid Rs. 20,000); current liabilities Rs. 1,50,000. Quick ratio is:
questions.e: Quick assets = 3,00,000 - 80,000 - 20,000 = Rs. 2,00,000. Quick ratio = 2,00,000/1,50,000 = 1.33:1. Stock and prepaid expenses are excluded as not quickly realisable.

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: A company issues 10,000 equity shares of Rs. 10 at a premium of Rs. 4, payable Rs. 6 on application (incl. premium). Application money received for 12,000 shares; pro-rata allotment to 10,000. Excess application money adjusted towards allotment is:
questions.e: Excess applications = 2,000 shares x Rs. 6 = Rs. 12,000, adjusted against allotment due. Application Rs. 6 includes Rs. 2 premium (6 = 4 face portion + 2 premium? Premium total 4: application takes 2). Excess = 2,000 x 6 = 12,000 either way.

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: A company cannot issue shares at a discount except:
o: Any equity shares with board approval
questions.e: Section 53 prohibits issue of shares at a discount, with the only exception being sweat equity shares issued under Section 54. Bonus shares are capitalised from reserves, not issued at discount.

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: Forfeited shares were originally issued at par. On reissue at a premium, the premium is credited to:
questions.e: Any premium on reissue of forfeited shares is securities premium (Section 52), credited to Securities Premium Account. The forfeiture balance left after reissue discount goes to Capital Reserve.

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: After reissue of all forfeited shares, the balance in Share Forfeiture Account is transferred to:
questions.e: The leftover forfeiture balance is a capital profit transferred to Capital Reserve. It can never be used for dividends.

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: ESOPs (Employee Stock Option Plans) are accounted as:
o: Employee compensation cost over the vesting period
questions.e: Compensation cost equal to fair value of options is recognised over the vesting period ( debit Employee Compensation, credit Stock Options Outstanding). It reflects service received from employees.

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: Debentures of Rs. 5,00,000 are redeemed out of profits by conversion into equity shares. The entry for the transfer to DRR (assume 25% requirement) is:
o: No DRR is required when debentures are redeemed by conversion into shares
questions.e: Debenture Redemption Reserve is not required where debentures are redeemed by conversion into shares -- conversion is exempt. DRR applies to cash redemptions out of profits (check current applicability thresholds in the Companies Act rules).

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: Own debentures purchased by the company for Rs. 95,000 (face value Rs. 1,00,000) and immediately cancelled give a profit of:
questions.e: Profit on cancellation of own debentures = 1,00,000 - 95,000 = Rs. 5,000, a capital profit transferred to Capital Reserve, not distributable as dividend.

questions.subject: Intangibles (AS-26)
questions.q: A firm purchased goodwill for Rs. 2,00,000. As per AS-26 it should be:
o: Amortised over its useful life, not exceeding 10 years unless rebutted
questions.e: AS-26 (Intangible Assets): purchased goodwill is amortised over its useful life, presumed not to exceed 10 years unless persuasive evidence otherwise. Self-generated goodwill is never recognised.

questions.subject: Intangibles (AS-26)
questions.q: Research expenditure under AS-26 is:
questions.e: AS-26: research costs are expensed when incurred since future benefits are uncertain. Development costs may be capitalised only if strict recognition criteria (technical feasibility, intent, measurable cost, probable benefits) are met.

questions.subject: Fixed assets
questions.q: A machine is acquired on deferred payment: cash price Rs. 4,00,000, total instalments Rs. 4,60,000. The asset is recorded at:
questions.e: AS-10/AS-6 cost principle: the asset is recorded at its cash price equivalent (Rs. 4,00,000); the Rs. 60,000 difference is interest charged to P&L over the credit period. Recording at 4,60,000 would overstate the asset.

questions.subject: Government grants (AS-12)
questions.q: Government grant related to a depreciable asset, under AS-12, may be:
o: Deducted from the asset's cost or treated as deferred income
Credited to P&L in the year of receipt
questions.e: AS-12 offers two treatments for asset-related grants: deduct from gross cost (reducing depreciation base) or credit deferred income amortised over the asset's life. Grants are not credited straight to P&L or capital reserve on receipt.

questions.subject: Investments (AS-13)
questions.q: An investment classified as long-term is carried at:
o: Cost, with provision for other-than-temporary decline
Lower of cost and market value
questions.e: AS-13: long-term investments are carried at cost; provision is made only for decline considered other than temporary. Current investments are carried at lower of cost and fair value.

questions.subject: Borrowing costs (AS-16)
questions.q: Borrowing costs directly attributable to a qualifying asset are, under AS-16:
o: Capitalised as part of the asset's cost
questions.e: AS-16: borrowing costs on a qualifying asset (needing substantial time to get ready) are capitalised during the construction period. Other borrowing costs are expensed. Capitalisation is suspended during extended interruptions.

questions.subject: Segment reporting (AS-17)
questions.q: Segment reporting under AS-17 applies to:
o: Enterprises whose securities are listed or which are in the process of listing
questions.e: AS-17 applies to enterprises with listed (or to-be-listed) equity or debt securities and certain large enterprises. It requires primary/secondary segment disclosures by business and geography.

questions.subject: Related parties (AS-18)
questions.q: Related party disclosures under AS-18 do NOT apply to:
o: Transactions between state-controlled enterprises merely because of state control
questions.e: AS-18 exempts state-controlled enterprises from disclosing dealings with other state-controlled enterprises. Holding-subsidiary, KMP and associate relationships are all within its scope.

questions.subject: Leases (AS-19)
questions.q: Under AS-19, in a finance lease the lessee recognises:
o: An asset and a liability at the lower of fair value and PV of minimum lease payments
questions.e: AS-19: a finance lease transfers substantially all risks and rewards, so the lessee capitalises the asset with a matching liability. Operating lease rentals are expensed straight-line over the term.

questions.subject: EPS (AS-20)
questions.q: Earnings per share (AS-20): net profit Rs. 12,00,000; 4,00,000 equity shares outstanding; 1,00,000 potential convertible debentures (each convertible to 1 share). Diluted EPS is:
questions.e: Basic EPS = 12,00,000/4,00,000 = Rs. 3. Diluted shares = 5,00,000; diluted EPS = 12,00,000/5,00,000 = Rs. 2.40 (ignoring post-tax interest adjustment for simplicity). Diluted EPS can never exceed basic EPS.

questions.subject: EPS (AS-20)
questions.q: A company declares a 1:1 bonus issue. Its EPS for the prior year presented comparatively must be:
questions.e: AS-20: bonus issues and splits are treated as if outstanding from the beginning of the earliest period presented, so comparative EPS is restated. This keeps per-share trends meaningful.

questions.subject: Taxes on income (AS-22)
questions.q: Deferred tax asset is recognised, under AS-22, only when:
o: The company is profitable this year
There is reasonable/virtual certainty of realisation
questions.e: AS-22: DTA on timing differences needs reasonable certainty; on unabsorbed depreciation/losses it needs virtual certainty supported by convincing evidence. Prudence restricts DTA recognition.

questions.subject: Final accounts
questions.q: A bills payable of Rs. 25,000 is shown under:
questions.e: Bills payable maturing within the operating cycle/12 months are current liabilities (trade payables). Only bills maturing beyond 12 months would be non-current.

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: Calls in arrears are shown in the balance sheet:
questions.e: Calls in arrears reduce the called-up capital presentation (shown by deduction). They are not an asset; the company has a claim but presents net paid-up capital.

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: Preliminary expenses written off appear in:
o: Profit & Loss Account as an expense
questions.e: Preliminary expenses are amortised to P&L (often via securities premium or P&L write-off). Unamortised balance sits under 'other non-current assets' until fully written off.

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: Securities premium of Rs. 2,00,000 and preliminary expenses of Rs. 50,000. Maximum preliminary expenses that can be written off against premium:
questions.e: Section 52 permits writing off preliminary expenses against securities premium up to the actual preliminary expenses incurred (Rs. 50,000 here). The remaining premium stays in the Securities Premium Account.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: A partner's capital is fixed. His share of profit is credited to:
questions.e: With fixed capitals, all appropriations (profit share, interest, salary) go to the partners' current accounts; capital accounts change only for fresh capital or permanent withdrawals. Fluctuating capitals take everything to capital accounts.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: The Partnership Act, 1932 does NOT apply to:
o: A company registered under the Companies Act
A firm of 20 partners in banking
questions.e: The Partnership Act governs partnership firms; companies are governed by the Companies Act, 2013. Registration of a firm is optional under the Partnership Act (though unregistered firms face disabilities in suits).

questions.subject: Amalgamation concepts
questions.q: On amalgamation in the nature of merger, purchase consideration is discharged:
o: Wholly by issue of equity shares of the transferee
questions.e: AS-14: in a merger, consideration is discharged wholly by equity shares (except cash for fractional shares). Partly-cash consideration indicates a purchase, not a merger. (Foundation keeps this at concept level.)

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: An offer lapses if it is not accepted within:
o: The time prescribed, or a reasonable time if none is prescribed
questions.e: Section 6: an offer lapses after the prescribed time, or after a reasonable time where none is fixed. What is reasonable depends on the facts; no fixed statutory period applies to all offers.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Communication of acceptance is complete as against the proposer when:
o: It is put in a course of transmission so as to be out of the acceptor's power
It comes to the proposer's knowledge
questions.e: Section 4: acceptance is complete against the proposer when posted (out of acceptor's power), but complete against the acceptor only when it comes to the proposer's knowledge. This asymmetry is a favourite exam point.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: A proposal made by words spoken is called:
questions.e: Section 9: express promises arise from words spoken or written; implied promises from conduct. A counter offer is a rejection-plus-new-offer, and a standing offer (tender) invites future orders.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Acceptance of a general offer (e.g., a reward advertisement) is complete:
o: By performance of the stipulated act, no prior communication needed
Only after the offeror is informed in advance
questions.e: In Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co., performance of the condition (using the smoke ball as directed) was acceptance of the general offer. No prior notice of acceptance is needed for such offers.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Consideration must be:
o: At the desire of the promisor
questions.e: Section 2(d): consideration is an act/abstinence/promise done at the desire of the promisor. It need not be adequate (courts don't weigh value), may be past/present/future, and need not be in money.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: 'No consideration, no contract' -- which is a valid exception?
o: A purely oral promise to gift Rs. 10,000
A promise to pay for a past voluntary service made orally
A time-barred debt promise made orally
A written and registered agreement based on natural love and affection
questions.e: Section 25 exceptions: (1) written + registered agreements out of natural love and affection between near relations; (2) compensation for past voluntary service; (3) promise to pay a time-barred debt -- but (2) and (3) must be in writing and signed. An oral gift promise is unenforceable.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: A minor's agreement is:
o: Valid if for necessaries only in all cases
questions.e: Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose: a minor's agreement is absolutely void from the beginning. Only supply of necessaries binds the minor's property (Section 68), not the minor personally.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: A person of unsound mind may contract:
questions.e: Section 12: a person usually of unsound mind but occasionally sound may contract during lucid intervals; one usually sound but occasionally unsound may not contract while unsound. Capacity tracks actual soundness at the time.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Coercion under Section 15 includes:
o: Threatening to commit an act forbidden by the Indian Penal Code
A threat to file a civil suit
questions.e: Coercion = committing or threatening to commit an act forbidden by the IPC, or unlawful detention of property, to compel consent. A threat of an ordinary civil suit is not coercion.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Undue influence requires:
o: One party dominating the will of the other plus an unconscionable bargain
questions.e: Section 16: undue influence needs (a) a relationship enabling domination of will (parent-child, doctor-patient, fiduciary, etc.) and (b) use of that position to obtain an unfair advantage. Dominance is presumed in listed relationships.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: A contract caused by fraud is:
o: Voidable at the option of the deceived party
questions.e: Sections 17-19: fraud, coercion, undue influence and misrepresentation make the contract voidable at the victim's option. Mistake (bilateral, as to essential fact) can make it void.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Silence as to facts amounts to fraud when:
o: There is a duty to speak, as in contracts of utmost good faith
questions.e: Mere silence is not fraud (Section 17, Explanation); it becomes fraud where a duty to speak exists -- uberrima fides contracts like insurance -- or where silence is equivalent to speech.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: An agreement in restraint of marriage is:
questions.e: Section 26: every agreement restraining the marriage of any person (other than a minor) is void. Reasonableness of the restraint is irrelevant, unlike partial restraints of trade.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: An agreement by way of wager is:
o: Illegal in all cases with punishment
Void, and no suit lies to recover winnings
questions.e: Section 30: wagering agreements are void; no suit can be brought to recover anything won on a wager. Wagering is void but not illegal per se (collateral transactions may survive, except in some states).

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: A contingent contract (Section 31) is:
o: A contract to do or not do something if an uncertain future event happens or does not happen
questions.e: Contingent contracts depend on a collateral uncertain event (e.g., insurance). They are valid and enforceable when the event occurs; wagering agreements depend on the event itself as the very subject and are void.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: A quasi-contract arises:
o: Only by court decree after trial
By operation of law, without any agreement between parties
questions.e: Sections 68-72 impose obligations resembling contract where none was agreed -- e.g., necessaries supplied to an incapable person, money paid by mistake -- preventing unjust enrichment by operation of law.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Money paid by mistake must be repaid under:
questions.e: Section 72: a person to whom money is paid or anything delivered by mistake or under coercion must repay/return it. Section 73 covers compensation for breach; 74 covers stipulated penalties.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: In a contract of indemnity, the liability of the indemnifier arises:
o: When the loss actually occurs to the indemnity-holder
questions.e: Indemnity (Section 124) promises to save another from loss caused by the promisor's conduct or a third party's; liability crystallises when loss is suffered. The indemnity-holder's rights (Section 125) include damages, costs and sums paid.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: A contract of guarantee requires:
o: Three parties: creditor, principal debtor and surety
questions.e: Section 126: guarantee = promise to discharge the liability of a third person (principal debtor) on his default, involving creditor, principal debtor and surety. Consideration for the principal debtor suffices for the surety.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: A surety is discharged if the creditor:
o: Demands payment from the surety first
questions.e: Sections 133-139: release of the principal debtor, variance in terms without surety's consent, or compounding with the debtor discharges the surety. Merely suing the debtor or taking more security does not.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: In bailment, the bailee must:
o: Return the goods only after payment
Take reasonable care of the goods as a person of ordinary prudence would
Insure the goods in all cases
questions.e: Section 151: the bailee must take as much care as a person of ordinary prudence would of his own goods of similar bulk, quality and value. Unauthorised use (Section 154) makes him liable for loss even by accident.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: A pledge is:
o: A guarantee by a third party
Bailment of goods as security for a debt
questions.e: Section 172: pledge (pawn) is bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise. The pawnee has a right of retainer and, on default, may sell after reasonable notice.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: An agent's authority to bind the principal arises from:
o: A written deed in all cases
questions.e: Section 182: agency is created by express or implied agreement; no consideration is necessary for agency (Section 185), and writing is not mandatory except where the underlying act needs it.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: A sub-agent is properly appointed when:
o: The agent has express or implied authority to do so
questions.e: Section 190: an agent cannot delegate (delegatus non potest delegare) unless the ordinary custom of trade or the nature of agency permits. A properly appointed sub-agent binds the principal; otherwise the agent alone is liable.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Ratification of an unauthorised act by the principal:
o: Relates back to the date of the act
questions.e: Section 196: ratification (express or implied) relates back -- the agent's act becomes the principal's from the date it was done. The principal must have existed and had capacity then, and ratification must be of the whole act.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Damages for breach of contract are governed by the rule in:
questions.e: Section 73 embodies Hadley v Baxendale: only losses naturally arising in the usual course, or within the parties' contemplation when contracting, are recoverable. Remote/indirect losses are excluded; no damages for mental distress in commercial contracts ordinarily.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Liquidated damages under Section 74:
o: Require proof of actual loss in every case
Are recoverable as reasonable compensation not exceeding the stipulated sum, without proving actual loss
questions.e: Section 74: on breach where a sum is named (or penalty stipulated), the aggrieved party gets reasonable compensation up to the named sum without proving actual damage. Courts may reduce an extravagant penalty to reasonable compensation.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Specific performance of a contract may be granted when:
o: Damages are an inadequate remedy, e.g., sale of specific immovable property
questions.e: Under the Specific Relief Act, specific performance is granted where compensation in money is inadequate -- typically contracts for specific movable/immovable property. Personal-service and purely monetary contracts are excluded.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: A contract is discharged by novation when:
o: The parties substitute a new contract for the old with mutual consent
questions.e: Section 62: novation, rescission and alteration discharge the original contract by substituting a new one, requiring all parties' consent. The old contract's obligations end and new ones begin.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: If time is not of the essence, failure to perform on time makes the contract:
o: Voidable at the promisee's option, not void
questions.e: Section 55: where time is of the essence, delay voids the contract at the promisee's option; otherwise the promisee can claim compensation for loss caused by delay but cannot avoid the contract.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: An anticipatory breach occurs when:
o: Payment is delayed by one day
A party repudiates the contract before the due date of performance
questions.e: Anticipatory breach = refusal to perform before performance is due (express repudiation or disabling conduct). The promisee may sue immediately or wait till the due date, keeping the contract alive at his risk.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: A tender (standing offer) is:
o: A firm offer binding the inviter
An invitation to offer, not an offer itself
questions.e: A tender invites offers; the submitted bid is the offer, accepted by a work order. A standing offer (running contract) becomes a series of contracts as orders are placed. Price lists and auction invitations are similar invitations.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Cross offers (identical offers crossing in post) result in:
o: No contract, as neither is acceptance of the other
questions.e: Two identical offers crossing in the post do not form a contract because neither party accepted the other's offer -- acceptance requires communication in response to an offer (Tinn v Hoffmann).

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: An agreement without consideration is void except where it is:
o: In writing, registered, and made out of natural love and affection between near relatives
questions.e: Section 25's first exception needs all three: writing, registration, and natural love and affection between parties in near relation. Past voluntary service and time-barred debt promises are separate written-and-signed exceptions.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: past consideration is valid consideration when:
o: The act was done at the promisor's desire and he later promises to pay
The act was voluntary and unrelated
questions.e: Exception 2 to Section 25: a promise to compensate, wholly or partly, for something already done voluntarily for the promisor is enforceable -- but the promise must be in writing and signed, and the past act must have been at the promisor's desire or voluntary for him.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: A contract with a minor for necessaries:
o: Binds the minor's property, not the minor personally
questions.e: Section 68: necessaries supplied to a person incapable of contracting (minor/lunatic) are recoverable from his property, not personally. What counts as necessaries depends on the minor's station in life.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: A mistake of law of the land:
o: Does not excuse the contract (ignorantia juris non excusat)
questions.e: Section 21: mistake as to Indian law does not make a contract voidable; everyone is presumed to know the law. Mistake of foreign law is treated like mistake of fact.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Bilateral mistake as to an essential fact makes the agreement:
questions.e: Section 20: where both parties are under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement, it is void. Unilateral mistake generally does not avoid a contract (exceptions: identity, nature of document).

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: An agreement to do an impossible act is:
questions.e: Section 56: agreements to do impossible acts are void (initial impossibility). Supervening impossibility (doctrine of frustration) -- e.g., subject matter destroyed -- excuses performance and discharges the contract.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: The doctrine of frustration does NOT apply when:
o: The impossibility is self-induced by the promisor
A person essential for performance dies
War breaks out making performance illegal
questions.e: Section 56 frustration excuses only supervening impossibility not caused by the promisor. Self-induced impossibility, or mere commercial hardship/increased cost, does not discharge the contract.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Quantum meruit claims arise when:
o: There is a fully performed valid contract
Work is done under a contract that becomes void or is prevented
questions.e: Quantum meruit ('as much as deserved') allows reasonable remuneration where a contract is discharged, becomes void, or one party prevents performance after part execution. It is restitutionary, not contractual damages.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: A continuing guarantee is revoked by:
o: Death of the surety as to all past transactions automatically
Notice to the creditor as to future transactions
questions.e: Section 130: a continuing guarantee (for a series of transactions) may be revoked by the surety by notice to the creditor regarding future transactions. Death revokes it for future transactions unless there is a contrary contract (Section 131).

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: The pawnee's right on default includes:
o: Retaining the goods and selling them after reasonable notice
questions.e: Section 176: on default the pawnee may sue for the debt while retaining the goods, or sell them after reasonable notice and sue for any balance. Sale proceeds beyond the debt go to the pawnor.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: A gratuitous bailment is terminated by:
o: Death of the bailor or bailee
questions.e: Section 162: gratuitous bailment ends on the death of bailor or bailee. The bailor may also terminate before the agreed term, compensating the bailee for loss exceeding benefit (Section 159).

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: An agent who acts beyond authority:
o: Is personally liable to third parties
Binds the principal in all cases
questions.e: Sections 227-228: acts beyond authority don't bind the principal unless ratified; the agent is personally liable to third parties (implied warranty of authority). Only the principal can ratify.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Del credere agency is one where:
o: The agent guarantees the solvency of third parties he contracts with
questions.e: A del credere agent, for extra commission, guarantees the principal against the third party's default/insolvency. He remains an agent (not a surety) but bears the credit risk he underwrote.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Notice of revocation of agency is complete:
o: As against the agent when it comes to his knowledge; as against third parties when communicated to them
questions.e: Revocation follows the communication rules: complete against the agent when it reaches his knowledge, and against third parties only when communicated to them (Sections 201-208). Prior authorised acts remain binding.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: An agency coupled with interest is:
questions.e: Section 202: where the agent has an interest in the subject matter (e.g., authority to sell goods to recover his dues), the agency cannot be revoked to the prejudice of that interest, and survives the principal's death/insanity.

questions.subject: Sale of Goods Act
questions.q: A 'sale' differs from an 'agreement to sell' because in a sale:
o: Property in the goods passes immediately to the buyer
The price is always paid at once
questions.e: Section 4, Sale of Goods Act, 1930: in a sale, property transfers at once; in an agreement to sell, transfer happens on a future date or condition. Risk prima facie follows property (Section 26).

questions.subject: Sale of Goods Act
questions.q: If an agreement to sell is breached by the seller, the buyer's remedy is:
o: Damages for non-delivery; he cannot recover the goods as owner
Recovery of the goods as owner
questions.e: Since property hasn't passed, the buyer is not owner and sues for damages for non-delivery (Section 57). Only after property passes can he sue for the goods themselves.

questions.subject: Sale of Goods Act
questions.q: Goods that are identified and agreed upon at the time of contract are:
questions.e: Section 2(14): specific goods are identified and agreed upon when the contract is made. Unascertained/future goods become specific only on identification/ascertainment. Risk and property rules differ sharply between them.

questions.subject: Sale of Goods Act
questions.q: A condition in a sale of goods is:
o: A stipulation essential to the main purpose, breach of which allows repudiation
A minor stipulation allowing only damages
questions.e: Section 12: a condition is essential; its breach lets the buyer repudiate and claim damages. A warranty is collateral -- breach gives damages only. A condition may be waived or treated as warranty by the buyer.

questions.subject: Sale of Goods Act
questions.q: The doctrine of caveat emptor means:
o: The buyer can always return goods
Let the buyer beware -- he must examine the goods
questions.e: Caveat emptor: the buyer must satisfy himself about quality/fitness, with exceptions -- seller's active concealment, goods bought by description, fitness for a stated purpose made known, and merchantable quality in described goods.

questions.subject: Sale of Goods Act
questions.q: Implied condition as to fitness for purpose arises when:
o: The buyer makes known the purpose and relies on the seller's skill, and the seller deals in such goods
questions.e: Section 16(1): fitness is implied where the buyer expressly/impliedly makes known the particular purpose, relies on the seller's skill/judgment, and the seller ordinarily deals in those goods. Patent defects the buyer examined are excluded.

questions.subject: Sale of Goods Act
questions.q: Under 'nemo dat quod non habet':
o: No one can give a better title than he himself has
The seller need not have title
The buyer always gets good title
questions.e: Section 27 states nemo dat -- a non-owner generally cannot pass title. Exceptions: sale by mercantile agent, co-owner, person with voidable title before avoidance, seller/buyer in possession, and estoppel.

questions.subject: Sale of Goods Act
questions.q: A buyer who obtains goods under a voidable title (not yet avoided) passes:
o: Good title to a bona fide purchaser for value without notice
Title only with the seller's consent
questions.e: Section 27 exception (and Section 29): a person with voidable title passes good title if the title hasn't been avoided and the buyer acts in good faith without notice. Fraud makes title voidable, not void.

questions.subject: Sale of Goods Act
questions.q: An unpaid seller's right of lien can be exercised:
o: Only while he is in possession of the goods
questions.e: Section 46-49: lien needs possession; it is lost on delivery, waiver, or when the buyer tenders price. Lien is for the price of the goods sold, not other dues.

questions.subject: Sale of Goods Act
questions.q: The unpaid seller's right of stoppage in transit arises when:
o: The buyer becomes insolvent and the goods are still in transit
The buyer delays payment by one day
questions.e: Sections 50-52: on buyer's insolvency, the unpaid seller may stop goods in transit and resume possession. Transit ends when the buyer or his agent takes delivery; mere arrival at destination without taking delivery doesn't end transit.

questions.subject: Sale of Goods Act
questions.q: Risk prima facie passes with:
questions.e: Section 26: risk follows property unless otherwise agreed. If delivery is delayed by either party's fault, the party at fault bears the risk of loss that wouldn't otherwise have occurred.

questions.subject: Sale of Goods Act
questions.q: Delivery of goods to a carrier for transmission to the buyer is prima facie:
questions.e: Section 39: handing goods to a carrier (named or usual) for the buyer is prima facie delivery to the buyer, making the carrier the buyer's agent for custody; the seller must make a reasonable contract with the carrier.

questions.subject: Sale of Goods Act
questions.q: If the seller delivers a quantity less than contracted, the buyer may:
o: Accept and pay full price compulsorily
questions.e: Section 37: short delivery -- the buyer may reject; if he accepts, he pays at the contract rate. Excess delivery: he may reject the excess or accept all paying for the excess at contract rate.

questions.subject: Indian Partnership Act
questions.q: A partnership under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 requires:
o: A written deed in all cases
An agreement between persons to share profits of a business carried on by all or any acting for all
questions.e: Section 4: partnership = relation from agreement to share profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all. Registration is optional (with disabilities for unregistered firms); oral agreements suffice.

questions.subject: Indian Partnership Act
questions.q: The maximum number of partners in a firm is governed by:
questions.e: Section 464 of the Companies Act, 2013 caps associations/partnerships (beyond the prescribed number, commonly 50) unless registered as a company -- verify the current prescribed number in the rules. The Partnership Act itself sets no maximum.

questions.subject: Indian Partnership Act
questions.q: An unregistered firm suffers the disability that:
o: It cannot sue third parties to enforce contractual rights
Partners have no rights at all
questions.e: Section 69: an unregistered firm (or partner) cannot enforce contractual claims by suit against third parties, though third parties can sue the firm. Suits for dissolution/accounts and some statutory rights are exempted.

questions.subject: Indian Partnership Act
questions.q: A minor may be admitted to the benefits of an existing partnership:
questions.e: Section 30: a minor can be admitted to benefits (not full partnership) with all partners' consent. Within 6 months of majority (or gaining knowledge), he must elect to become or not become a partner, else he is deemed a partner.

questions.subject: Indian Partnership Act
questions.q: Every partner is liable for the firm's acts:
o: Jointly and severally with all other partners
Only if he signed the contract
Only to the extent of capital contributed
questions.e: Section 25: partners are jointly and severally liable for all acts of the firm done while he is a partner. A retiring partner can limit post-retirement liability by public notice (Sections 32, 72).

questions.subject: Indian Partnership Act
questions.q: A firm is dissolved compulsorily when:
o: All partners become insolvent or the business becomes unlawful
questions.e: Section 41: compulsory dissolution on all partners' insolvency (except one) or the business becoming unlawful. Retirement/admission merely reconstitutes the firm; Section 42 covers dissolution on contingencies.

questions.subject: Indian Partnership Act
questions.q: On dissolution, firm losses (including capital deficiencies) are borne:
o: First out of profits, then capital, then by partners in profit-sharing ratio
questions.e: Section 48: losses are paid first from profits, next from capital, lastly by partners individually in profit-sharing ratio. Assets are applied in order: outside creditors, partner advances, partner capital, then surplus shared.

questions.subject: Indian Partnership Act
questions.q: The authority of a partner to bind the firm is called:
questions.e: Section 18-19: every partner is an agent of the firm and co-partners for business purposes -- implied authority to bind the firm for acts usual in that business. Restrictions in the deed don't bind outsiders without knowledge.

questions.subject: Indian Partnership Act
questions.q: A partner's implied authority does NOT include:
o: Submitting a firm dispute to arbitration
questions.e: Section 19(2): unless custom/trade usage permits, implied authority excludes submitting disputes to arbitration, opening a bank account in his own name, compromising claims, withdrawing suits, admitting liability, or acquiring immovable property.

questions.subject: LLP Act
questions.q: A Limited Liability Partnership is:
o: A body corporate with perpetual succession and partners' liability limited to their agreed contribution
A company under the Companies Act
questions.e: LLP Act, 2008: an LLP is a body corporate (separate legal entity, perpetual succession); partners aren't liable for others' wrongful acts, liability limited to agreed contribution, except in fraud.

questions.subject: LLP Act
questions.q: Every LLP must have at least:
o: Two designated partners, one resident in India
questions.e: LLP Act: minimum two designated partners, at least one resident in India (stayed 180+ days in the preceding year -- verify current residency definition). Designated partners handle compliance and face penalties for defaults.

questions.subject: LLP Act
questions.q: A key difference between an LLP and a company is:
o: An LLP has no shareholders; ownership and management vest in partners
An LLP has no perpetual succession
questions.e: An LLP blends partnership flexibility with corporate personality: partners own and manage directly (no board/shareholder split), yet the LLP is a separate body corporate that can own property, sue and be sued.

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: A company is distinguished from a partnership mainly by:
o: Separate legal personality distinct from its members
questions.e: Salomon v Salomon: incorporation creates a separate legal person; members' liability is limited and the company survives membership changes. Partnerships lack separate personality (except LLP).

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: The Memorandum of Association contains:
o: The objects clause defining the company's permitted activities
questions.e: MOA is the company's charter: name, registered office, objects, liability, capital clauses. Acts beyond the objects are ultra vires and void. AOA contains internal regulations and is subordinate to the MOA.

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: The doctrine of indoor management (Royal British Bank v Turquand) protects:
o: Outsiders dealing in good faith who may assume internal procedures were followed
questions.e: Indoor management: outsiders needn't verify internal compliance (board resolutions, quorums) if they dealt in good faith. Exceptions: knowledge of irregularity, forgery, or circumstances putting one on inquiry.

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: A private company under the Companies Act, 2013:
o: Restricts share transfer, limits members to 200, and prohibits public invitation
questions.e: Section 2(68): a private company restricts transferability, limits members to 200 (excluding past/present employees), and prohibits public invitations for securities. One Person Company is a private-company variant.

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: The minimum number of members for a public company is:
questions.e: Section 3: a public company needs at least 7 members (private: 2; OPC: 1). Falling below the minimum can expose members to personal liability for debts after 6 months in some situations -- verify current provisions.

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: A prospectus must state:
o: Material information enabling investors to decide, including risk factors and objects of the issue
questions.e: Sections 26-27: a prospectus discloses objects, financials, risk factors, management, and litigation. Misstatements attract civil/criminal liability (Sections 34-35); Golden Rule: strict compliance with disclosure.

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: The first auditor of a company (other than a government company) is appointed by:
o: The Board within 30 days of registration
questions.e: Section 139: the Board appoints the first auditor within 30 days of registration; failing that, members do so within 90 days at an EGM. Subsequent auditors are appointed at each AGM for 5-year terms (ratification requirement removed).

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: An Annual General Meeting must be held:
o: Within 6 months of the financial year-end, with not more than 15 months between AGMs
questions.e: Section 96: AGM within 6 months of FY close; gap between AGMs max 15 months (extendable by 3 months by the Registrar). First AGM may be within 9 months of first FY close.

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: Ordinary business at an AGM includes:
o: Declaration of dividend, appointment of directors and auditors
questions.e: Section 102: ordinary business = accounts, dividend declaration, director appointments/reappointments, auditor appointment/fixation of remuneration. Everything else is special business needing an explanatory statement.

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: A special resolution requires:
o: At least 3/4th majority of votes cast
questions.e: Section 114: special resolution needs votes in favour >= 3 times votes against (75% of votes cast). Matters like altering MOA/AOA, buy-back, and winding up need special resolutions.

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: Debenture holders are:
questions.e: Debenture holders lend to the company -- they are creditors with fixed interest, ranking ahead of shareholders on winding up. Shareholders are owners (members).

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: The Doctrine of Ultra Vires provides that:
o: Acts beyond the objects clause are void and cannot be ratified
Acts beyond the AOA are void
questions.e: Ashbury Railway Carriage Co. v Riche: ultra vires (beyond MOA objects) acts are void ab initio and cannot be ratified even unanimously. Intra vires but irregular acts may be ratified.

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: A company limited by guarantee is one where:
o: Members undertake to contribute a fixed sum on winding up
questions.e: Members' liability is limited to the guaranteed amount payable on winding up; often used for non-profits (Section 8 companies). Liability arises only on winding up, not during operations.

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: Which company need NOT hold an AGM?
questions.e: Section 96 exempts OPCs from AGMs (and from Section 98/100-111 meeting provisions generally). All other companies must hold AGMs; small companies get some relaxations but not this one.

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: The quorum for a public company's general meeting (members personally present) is:
questions.e: Section 103: quorum is 5 (<=1000 members), 15 (1000-5000), 30 (>5000) for public companies; 2 for private companies. Business transacted without quorum is invalid.

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: Proxy provisions do NOT apply to:
questions.e: Section 105 excludes OPCs from proxy rules (a single member needs no proxy). Listed companies additionally face e-voting and postal ballot requirements for prescribed matters.

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: A director is disqualified under Section 164 if:
o: He holds shares in the company
He is of unsound mind or an undischarged insolvent
questions.e: Section 164 disqualifications include unsound mind, undischarged insolvency, pending insolvency application, convictions with >=6 months imprisonment, and non-filing of financial statements/returns for 3 years. Age 70 needs special resolution for appointment, not disqualification.

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: Independent directors are required for:
o: Prescribed classes of listed and large public companies
questions.e: Section 149: prescribed listed companies and large public companies (paid-up capital/turnover/borrowings thresholds -- verify current Rule 4 thresholds) must have independent directors (1/3rd or 2 for listed). They bring objective oversight.

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: CSR (Section 135) applies to companies meeting thresholds, which must spend:
o: At least 2% of average net profits of the last 3 financial years
questions.e: Section 135: companies meeting net worth/turnover/profit thresholds (verify current limits) must spend >=2% of average net profits of the preceding 3 years on CSR; unspent amounts have specified transfer rules.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: A contract with a minor is void; however, a minor can be:
questions.e: A minor can benefit as promisee (e.g., receive a gift, be a payee) and can act as an agent binding the principal (though not personally liable). He cannot be a promisor bound personally nor a full partner.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Consideration may move from:
o: The promisee or any other person
questions.e: Indian law (unlike English law) allows consideration to move from the promisee or any other person (Chinnaya v Ramayya) -- but a stranger to the contract cannot sue on it (privity of contract).

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Privity of contract means:
o: Only parties to a contract can sue on it
Anyone can sue on any contract
questions.e: Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre v Selfridge: a stranger to the contract cannot enforce it, even if consideration moved from him. Exceptions: trusts, family settlements, assignment, agency, and covenants running with land.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: An agreement collateral to a wagering agreement is:
questions.e: Wagering agreements are void under Section 30 but not illegal per se, so collateral transactions (e.g., a loan to pay a bet) remain enforceable in most states -- Bombay is a notable exception where they are void.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Time is presumed to be of the essence in:
questions.e: In mercantile contracts time is generally of the essence; in sale of immovable property, time is ordinarily not of the essence unless expressly stated (Section 55 interpretation, Gomathinayagam Pillai v Pallaniswami Nadar).

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Appropriation of payments (Clayton's case) applies when:
o: The debtor does not specify appropriation and the creditor also does not -- payments apply to earliest debts
questions.e: Sections 59-61: debtor may appropriate at payment; failing that, the creditor may; failing both, appropriation is in order of time (earliest debt first), or proportionately if same date. This is the rule in Clayton's case.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: A bailee's lien is:
o: A particular lien -- only for charges due on those goods
A general lien in all cases
questions.e: Section 170: the bailee has a particular lien -- he may retain only the goods bailed for charges due on them. Bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys and policy-brokers enjoy a general lien (Section 171).

questions.subject: Sale of Goods Act
questions.q: The unpaid seller's right of resale arises when:
o: Goods are perishable, or after notice of intention to resell on buyer's default
questions.e: Section 54: the unpaid seller in possession may resell where goods are perishable, or after giving notice of intention to resell and the buyer still defaults; he can then recover damages for the loss on resale.

questions.subject: Sale of Goods Act
questions.q: Where goods are sold by description, there is an implied condition that:
o: The goods correspond with the description
questions.e: Section 15: sale by description implies the goods shall correspond with the description; where the buyer hasn't seen them, they must also be of merchantable quality (Section 16(2)).

questions.subject: Sale of Goods Act
questions.q: A sale by sample implies that:
o: The bulk corresponds with the sample and the buyer can compare
questions.e: Section 17: sale by sample implies (a) bulk corresponds with sample in quality, (b) buyer gets reasonable opportunity to compare, (c) goods are free from defects making them unmerchantable that aren't apparent on examination.

questions.subject: Sale of Goods Act
questions.q: The Sale of Goods Act, 1930 applies to:
o: Movable goods (excluding actionable claims and money)
questions.e: Section 2(7): 'goods' means movable property except actionable claims and money; includes stock, shares, growing crops, and things attached to land agreed to be severed. Immovable property is outside the Act.

questions.e: PV = 50000/1.1^3 = Rs. 37,566. Discounting reverses compounding.

questions.e: 2 distinct letters: 2! = 2 arrangements.

questions.e: 5 distinct books: 5! = 120 arrangements.

questions.e: The standard limit lim(x->0) sin x / x = 1, fundamental in calculus.

questions.subject: Central tendency

questions.e: Mean = sum/n = 90/5 = 18.

questions.subject: Central tendency
questions.q: The median of 8, 3, 11, 5, 9 is:
questions.e: Ordered: 3, 5, 8, 9, 11. Middle (3rd) value = 8.

questions.subject: Central tendency
questions.q: The mode of 4, 6, 4, 7, 4, 9 is:
questions.e: Mode = most frequent value: 4 occurs 3 times.

questions.subject: Central tendency
