questions.e: Karl Pearson's empirical relation: Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean, valid for moderately skewed distributions.

questions.subject: Central tendency
questions.q: Which average is most affected by extreme values?
questions.e: The arithmetic mean uses every value, so outliers pull it strongly. Median and mode are positional and resist extremes.

questions.subject: Central tendency
questions.q: The geometric mean of 4 and 9 is:
questions.e: GM = sqrt(4 x 9) = 6. GM suits ratios and growth rates.

questions.q: The standard deviation of 10, 12, 14, 16, 18 is closest to:
questions.e: Mean = 14; squared deviations average 8; SD = sqrt(8) = 2.83.

questions.subject: Dispersion
questions.q: The range of 15, 22, 9, 31, 18 is:
questions.e: Range = max - min = 31 - 9 = 22. It's the simplest but crudest dispersion measure.

questions.subject: Dispersion
questions.q: Coefficient of variation is:
questions.e: CV = (SD/mean) x 100%, a unit-free measure comparing variability across datasets with different means.

questions.subject: Dispersion

questions.subject: Probability

questions.e: One favourable outcome out of two equally likely: 1/2 = 0.5.

questions.subject: Probability
questions.q: The probability of rolling a 6 on a fair die is:
questions.e: One favourable face out of six: 1/6.

questions.subject: Probability
questions.q: If P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.5 with A, B independent, P(A and B) equals:
questions.e: For independent events, P(A n B) = P(A) x P(B) = 0.4 x 0.5 = 0.20.

questions.subject: Probability

questions.e: 3 favourable out of 5 total: 3/5.

questions.subject: Probability
questions.q: Two coins are tossed. Probability of getting exactly one head is:
questions.e: Outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT. Exactly one head: HT, TH = 2/4 = 1/2.

questions.subject: Probability

questions.e: Conditional probability: P(A|B) = P(A n B)/P(B), for P(B) > 0.

questions.e: Mutually exclusive: P(A n B) = 0, so P(A U B) = 0.3 + 0.4 = 0.7.

questions.e: When p = 0.5 (p = q), the binomial is symmetric. p > 0.5 skews left; p < 0.5 skews right.

questions.subject: Normal distribution

questions.e: Like all probability density curves, total area = 1.

questions.subject: Normal distribution

questions.e: Standard normal: mean = median = mode = 0, SD = 1. The curve is perfectly symmetric.

questions.subject: Normal distribution

questions.e: Arranging all n distinct objects: n! ways.

questions.subject: Probability

questions.subject: Nature & scope
questions.q: The central problems of an economy arise because of:
o: Scarcity of resources relative to unlimited wants
questions.e: Scarcity forces every economy to answer what, how and for whom to produce. Unlimited wants with limited resources is the root of all economic problems.

questions.subject: Nature & scope
questions.q: The 'what to produce' problem is concerned with:
o: The choice of goods and their quantities
questions.e: What to produce decides the goods-mix (consumer vs capital goods); 'how' chooses techniques; 'for whom' decides distribution among people.

questions.subject: PPC & opportunity cost
questions.q: A production possibility curve is concave to the origin because of:
questions.e: Concavity reflects increasing marginal opportunity cost: resources are specialised, so shifting them yields ever-larger sacrifices of the other good.

questions.subject: PPC & opportunity cost
questions.q: A point inside the PPC indicates:
questions.e: Inside the frontier, more of both goods is possible -- resources are idle or inefficient. Points on the curve are efficient; outside is unattainable with current resources.

questions.subject: PPC & opportunity cost
questions.q: An outward shift of the PPC is caused by:
questions.e: More/better resources or technology expand productive capacity, shifting the PPC out. Unemployment moves the economy inside the curve, not the curve itself.

questions.subject: Nature & scope
questions.q: Microeconomics deals with:
o: Individual units like a consumer or a firm
questions.e: Microeconomics studies individual decision-makers and single markets; macroeconomics studies aggregates like national income, inflation and unemployment.

questions.subject: Nature & scope
questions.q: Normative economics is concerned with:
questions.e: Positive economics describes what is; normative economics prescribes what ought to be, involving value judgments (e.g., 'inequality should be reduced').

questions.subject: Theory of demand
questions.q: The law of demand states that, other things equal:
o: Quantity demanded falls as price rises
Quantity demanded rises as price rises
questions.e: The first law of demand: an inverse price-quantity relation, ceteris paribus. A price change causes movement along the curve; other factors shift the curve.

questions.subject: Theory of demand
questions.q: An increase in consumer income will increase demand for:
questions.e: Normal goods have positive income elasticity; inferior goods (and Giffen goods) see demand fall as income rises.

questions.subject: Theory of demand
questions.q: A Giffen good is one for which:
o: Quantity demanded rises as price rises, due to a strong negative income effect
questions.e: Giffen goods are extreme inferior goods where the income effect outweighs substitution, giving an upward-sloping demand curve (e.g., staple foods for the very poor).

questions.subject: Theory of demand
questions.q: If the price of tea rises, the demand for coffee will:
questions.e: Tea and coffee are substitutes (positive cross elasticity): a rise in tea's price shifts coffee's demand curve right.

questions.subject: Theory of demand
questions.q: If the price of petrol rises, the demand for cars will:
questions.e: Petrol and cars are complements (negative cross elasticity): costlier petrol reduces car demand.

questions.subject: Theory of demand
questions.q: A change in price causes:
o: A shift of the demand curve
questions.e: Price changes move along the curve (extension/contraction). Non-price factors -- income, tastes, related prices, expectations -- shift the whole curve.

questions.subject: Theory of demand
questions.q: Market demand is derived by:
o: Horizontal summation of individual demand curves
questions.e: Market demand at each price is the sum of quantities all individuals demand -- horizontal summation.

questions.subject: Elasticity of demand
questions.q: Price elasticity of demand = -2 means:
o: A 2% price rise cuts quantity by 1%
A 1% price rise cuts quantity demanded by 2%
questions.e: Ed = % change in quantity / % change in price = -2: demand is elastic (|Ed| > 1), so a price rise reduces total revenue.

questions.subject: Elasticity of demand
questions.q: Demand for a product with many close substitutes is:
questions.e: More substitutes, larger budget share, and longer time horizons all raise elasticity. Necessities with no substitutes are inelastic.

questions.subject: Elasticity of demand
questions.q: If demand is perfectly inelastic, the demand curve is:
questions.e: Perfectly inelastic (Ed = 0): quantity unchanged whatever the price -- a vertical curve. Perfectly elastic is horizontal.

questions.subject: Elasticity of demand
questions.q: Total revenue is maximum when:
questions.e: TR rises while MR > 0, peaks where MR = 0 (unitary elasticity), then falls as MR turns negative.

questions.subject: Elasticity of demand
questions.q: Income elasticity of demand for inferior goods is:
questions.e: Inferior goods: quantity falls as income rises, so Ey < 0. Luxuries have Ey > 1; necessities 0 < Ey < 1.

questions.subject: Theory of supply
questions.q: The law of supply states that, other things equal:
o: Quantity supplied rises as price rises
Quantity supplied falls as price rises
questions.e: Producers offer more at higher prices -- an upward-sloping supply curve. Input costs, technology and taxes shift the curve.

questions.subject: Theory of supply
questions.q: An improvement in technology will:
o: Shift the supply curve to the right
Shift the supply curve to the left
questions.e: Better technology lowers cost, so firms supply more at each price -- a rightward shift. Higher input prices shift it left.

questions.subject: Consumer behaviour
questions.q: Total utility is maximum when:
questions.e: TU rises while MU > 0, peaks where MU = 0, then falls as MU turns negative -- the basis of the law of diminishing marginal utility.

questions.subject: Consumer behaviour
questions.q: The law of diminishing marginal utility states:
o: MU falls as consumption of the good increases
questions.e: Successive units yield smaller additional satisfaction (ceteris paribus). It explains why demand curves slope downward and the consumer's surplus.

questions.subject: Consumer behaviour
questions.q: Consumer equilibrium (cardinal approach) requires:
questions.e: The equi-marginal principle: the last rupee spent on each good must yield equal marginal utility. This maximises total utility within the budget.

questions.subject: Consumer behaviour
questions.q: An indifference curve is convex to the origin because of:
questions.e: Convexity reflects diminishing MRS: the consumer gives up less and less of Y for each extra X. Indifference curves slope down, never intersect, and lie farther for higher satisfaction.

questions.subject: Consumer behaviour
questions.q: The budget line shifts outward parallelly when:
o: Money income rises with prices unchanged
questions.e: Higher income (prices constant) expands the affordable set parallelly. A rise in X's price pivots the line inward on the X-axis.

questions.subject: Consumer behaviour
questions.q: Consumer's surplus is:
o: What the consumer is willing to pay minus what he actually pays
questions.e: Marshall's consumer surplus = total willingness to pay (area under demand curve) less actual expenditure -- a welfare measure of gain from trade.

questions.subject: Production
questions.q: The law of variable proportions states that as more of a variable input is added to fixed inputs:
o: MP first rises then falls, eventually becoming negative
questions.e: With fixed factors, MP initially rises (specialisation), then diminishes and turns negative. TP is maximum where MP = 0.

questions.subject: Production
questions.q: When marginal product exceeds average product:
questions.e: MP > AP pulls AP up; MP < AP pulls it down. AP is maximum where MP = AP (MP curve cuts AP at its peak).

questions.subject: Production
questions.q: The second stage of production ends where:
questions.e: Stage II (diminishing returns) runs from AP-maximum to TP-maximum (MP = 0). Rational producers operate in Stage II.

questions.subject: Production
questions.q: Increasing returns to scale occur when:
o: Output rises proportionately more than inputs
questions.e: IRS: doubling all inputs more than doubles output (specialisation, indivisibilities). Eventually decreasing returns set in.

questions.subject: Production
questions.q: An isoquant shows:
o: All input combinations yielding the same output
All output combinations with the same cost
questions.e: Isoquants are the producer's indifference curves: convex, downward sloping, non-intersecting, farther from origin = higher output.

questions.subject: Production
questions.q: The least-cost input combination is where:
o: The isoquant is tangent to the isocost line
questions.e: Equilibrium: MRTS = w/r (slope of isoquant equals slope of isocost). The expansion path joins such tangency points.

questions.subject: Cost
questions.q: In the short run, as output rises, average fixed cost:
questions.e: AFC = TFC/Q: spreading fixed cost over more units -- a rectangular hyperbola, always falling.

questions.subject: Cost
questions.q: The MC curve cuts the AC and AVC curves:
questions.e: MC crosses AC and AVC at their minima: when MC < AC, AC falls; when MC > AC, AC rises.

questions.subject: Cost
questions.q: The long-run average cost curve is:
questions.e: LRAC is the envelope of SRAC curves, U-shaped due to economies then diseconomies of scale. The minimum point is the optimum scale.

questions.subject: Cost
questions.q: Economies of scale arise from:
questions.e: Internal economies (technical, managerial, financial) lower unit cost as scale grows; beyond the optimum, diseconomies (coordination problems) raise it.

questions.subject: Cost
questions.q: Opportunity cost is:
questions.e: Opportunity cost = value of the best sacrificed alternative -- the economist's true cost concept, underlying PPC analysis.

questions.subject: Cost
questions.q: Sunk costs are:
questions.e: Sunk costs (already incurred, unrecoverable) should not affect rational forward-looking decisions; only marginal/incremental costs matter.

questions.subject: Perfect competition
questions.q: In perfect competition, the firm's demand curve is:
questions.e: A price-taking firm can sell any quantity at the market price, so its demand curve is horizontal at P = AR = MR.

questions.subject: Perfect competition
questions.q: A perfectly competitive firm maximises profit where:
questions.e: Profit maximisation: produce where MC = MR; with price-taking, MR = P. The second-order condition needs MC rising (cutting MR from below).

questions.subject: Perfect competition
questions.q: In the long run, a perfectly competitive firm earns:
questions.e: Free entry/exit wipes out supernormal profits: long-run equilibrium at P = MC = minimum LAC, yielding only normal profit.

questions.subject: Perfect competition
questions.q: The short-run supply curve of a competitive firm is:
o: The MC curve above minimum AVC
questions.e: The firm produces where P = MC provided P covers AVC; below minimum AVC it shuts down. Hence supply = MC above min AVC.

questions.subject: Perfect competition
questions.q: The shut-down point of a firm is where price equals:
questions.e: If P < min AVC, the firm loses more by operating than by shutting down (fixed costs are lost either way). Between min AVC and min AC it operates at a loss short-run.

questions.subject: Perfect competition
questions.q: Allocative efficiency (P = MC) is achieved in:
questions.e: Perfect competition gives both allocative efficiency (P = MC) and productive efficiency (P = min AC) in the long run -- the welfare benchmark.

questions.subject: Monopoly
questions.q: A monopolist's demand curve is:
questions.e: The monopolist is the industry: it faces the market demand curve, so to sell more it must cut price (MR < P).

questions.subject: Monopoly
questions.q: For a monopolist, marginal revenue is:
questions.e: Because price must fall on all units to sell an extra unit, MR < P (AR). The MR curve lies below AR and falls twice as fast for a linear demand.

questions.subject: Monopoly
questions.q: A monopolist maximises profit where:
questions.e: MC = MR is the universal profit-maximisation rule. Under monopoly this yields P > MC -- the source of deadweight loss.

questions.subject: Monopoly
questions.q: Price discrimination is profitable when:
o: Markets can be separated and elasticities differ
questions.e: Third-degree price discrimination needs separable markets, different elasticities, and no resale (arbitrage). The monopolist charges more where demand is less elastic.

questions.subject: Monopoly
questions.q: Deadweight loss of monopoly arises because:
o: Output is restricted below the competitive level (P > MC)
questions.e: Monopoly restricts output to where MR = MC, pricing above MC, so mutually beneficial trades are lost -- the welfare triangle.

questions.subject: Monopoly
questions.q: A natural monopoly exists when:
o: One firm can serve the market at lower cost than two (large economies of scale)
questions.e: With huge fixed costs and falling AC over market demand (utilities, railways), a single firm is cheapest; regulation or public ownership typically follows.

questions.subject: Monopolistic competition
questions.q: Monopolistic competition is characterised by:
o: Many sellers, differentiated products, free entry
questions.e: Chamberlin's model: many firms, product differentiation (branding, quality), free entry/exit. Each firm faces a downward-sloping but elastic demand curve.

questions.subject: Monopolistic competition
questions.q: In the long run, a monopolistically competitive firm earns:
questions.e: Free entry erodes supernormal profits; long-run tangency of demand with LAC gives normal profit, but with excess capacity (not at min LAC).

questions.subject: Monopolistic competition
questions.q: Excess capacity in monopolistic competition means:
o: Firms produce below the minimum-LAC output
questions.e: Long-run equilibrium occurs on the falling portion of LAC (demand tangent left of minimum), so output is below the least-cost scale -- the cost of product variety.

questions.subject: Monopolistic competition
questions.q: Non-price competition (advertising, branding) is most intense in:
questions.e: With differentiated products, firms compete on quality, advertising and service rather than price alone -- the hallmark of monopolistic competition and oligopoly.

questions.subject: Oligopoly
questions.q: Oligopoly is characterised by:
questions.e: A few dominant firms where each firm's decisions affect rivals, causing strategic behaviour -- price rigidity, cartels, and kinked demand analysis.

questions.subject: Oligopoly
questions.q: The kinked demand curve explains:
questions.e: Sweezy's kinked demand: rivals match price cuts but not hikes, making demand elastic above and inelastic below the kink -- MR has a gap, so costs can shift without changing price.

questions.subject: Oligopoly
questions.q: A cartel aims to:
o: Act as a collective monopolist, restricting output and raising price
questions.e: Cartels (e.g., OPEC) coordinate output/prices to earn monopoly profits, but each member is tempted to cheat -- hence their instability.

questions.subject: Oligopoly
questions.q: Price leadership in oligopoly means:
o: One dominant firm sets the price others follow
questions.e: The dominant or barometric firm announces price changes; others follow, achieving coordination without explicit collusion.

questions.subject: Monopoly
questions.q: In the short run, a monopoly firm may earn:
o: Supernormal profit, normal profit, or losses
questions.e: Short-run monopoly outcomes mirror competition except the demand curve slopes down: profit depends on demand vs cost, but losses can't persist if exit is possible long-run.

questions.subject: Market structures compared
questions.q: Which market form has the most elastic firm demand curve?
questions.e: Perfectly elastic (infinite) under perfect competition; highly elastic under monopolistic competition; less elastic for oligopoly/monopoly.

questions.subject: Market structures compared
questions.q: Productive efficiency (minimum average cost) is achieved long-run in:
questions.e: Only perfect competition forces P = min LAC long-run. Monopolistic competition has excess capacity; monopoly restricts output.

questions.subject: Market structures compared
questions.q: Barriers to entry are highest in:
questions.e: Monopoly sustains itself on barriers -- legal (patents), resource control, or large economies of scale. Free entry defines perfect/monopolistic competition.

questions.subject: Price determination
questions.q: Market equilibrium price is determined by:
questions.e: Equilibrium where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied; excess demand bids price up, excess supply pushes it down.

questions.subject: Price determination
questions.q: A price ceiling set below equilibrium causes:
questions.e: Capping price below equilibrium raises quantity demanded and cuts quantity supplied -- persistent shortage, often with black markets/rationing.

questions.subject: Price determination
questions.q: A price floor set above equilibrium causes:
questions.e: Minimum prices (e.g., MSP) above equilibrium induce excess supply that the government must purchase or stock.

questions.subject: Price determination
questions.q: An ad valorem tax on a good is:
questions.e: Ad valorem = 'on value' (e.g., 18% GST); specific tax is per unit. Tax incidence falls more on the side with less elastic response.

questions.subject: Price determination
questions.q: The incidence of a tax falls more heavily on:
o: The side of the market with less elastic response
questions.e: Tax burden is shared by relative elasticity: the less elastic side (buyers of necessities, sellers of perishables) bears more.

questions.subject: Business cycles
questions.q: The four phases of a business cycle are:
questions.e: The classic cycle: expansion/boom, contraction/recession, trough/depression, recovery -- repeating fluctuations around the growth trend.

questions.subject: Business cycles
questions.q: A recession is commonly identified as:
o: Two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP
questions.e: The popular rule of thumb: two successive quarterly declines in real GDP. Official dating (e.g., NBER) uses broader monthly indicators.

questions.subject: Business cycles
questions.q: During a recession, unemployment is typically:
questions.e: Falling demand cuts output and jobs -- cyclical unemployment rises above the natural rate; Okun's law links output gaps to unemployment.

questions.subject: Business cycles
questions.q: The multiplier effect means:
o: An initial spending change causes a larger total income change
questions.e: Multiplier = 1/(1-MPC) = 1/MPS: each spending round induces further consumption, amplifying the initial injection (subject to leakages).

questions.subject: Business cycles
questions.q: If MPC = 0.8, the investment multiplier is:
questions.e: k = 1/(1 - MPC) = 1/0.2 = 5. Higher MPC means less leakage into saving and a bigger multiplier.

questions.subject: Business cycles
questions.q: Automatic stabilisers include:
questions.e: Progressive taxes fall and transfers rise automatically in downturns, cushioning income without new legislation.

questions.subject: Business cycles
questions.q: Stagflation is:
o: High inflation with stagnant output and high unemployment
questions.e: Stagflation (1970s oil shocks) combines stagnation and inflation, typically from adverse supply shocks -- hard for demand policy to fix.

questions.subject: Business cycles
questions.q: The accelerator principle relates:
o: Induced investment to changes in output
questions.e: Accelerator: net investment responds to the rate of change of output/consumption -- volatile investment amplifies cycles (multiplier-accelerator interaction).

questions.subject: Business cycles
questions.q: Leading indicators of a business cycle include:
o: Stock prices, new orders and building permits
questions.e: Leading indicators turn before the economy; coincident (GDP, industrial production) move with it; lagging (unemployment, interest costs) follow.

questions.subject: Business cycles
questions.q: Monetary policy to fight a recession typically involves:
o: Cutting interest rates / expanding money supply
questions.e: Easier money lowers borrowing costs, stimulating investment and consumption. Contractionary policy (rate hikes) fights inflation.

questions.subject: Business cycles
questions.q: Fiscal policy to fight inflation typically involves:
questions.e: Contractionary fiscal policy reduces aggregate demand. Expansionary fiscal (spending up/taxes down) fights recessions.

questions.subject: Theory of demand
questions.q: The law of demand fails (exceptions include):
o: Giffen goods, prestige goods and expectations of further price changes
questions.e: Exceptions: Giffen goods (upward-sloping demand), Veblen/prestige goods, and speculative expectations where expected future prices drive current buying.

questions.subject: Elasticity of demand
questions.q: Cross elasticity of demand between substitutes is:
questions.e: Substitutes: positive (price rise of one raises demand for the other). Complements: negative. Unrelated goods: near zero.

questions.subject: Consumer behaviour
questions.q: If MUx/Px > MUy/Py, the consumer should:
o: Buy more of X and less of Y
questions.e: The last rupee on X yields more utility; shifting spending from Y to X raises total utility until equality is restored.

questions.subject: Production
questions.q: Returns to scale is a:
questions.e: Returns to scale vary all inputs together -- possible only in the long run. The law of variable proportions is its short-run counterpart.

questions.subject: Production
questions.q: The expansion path shows:
o: Least-cost input combinations at different output levels
questions.e: Joining tangency points of isoquants and isocosts, the expansion path traces cost-minimising input bundles as output grows; its shape reflects returns to scale.

questions.subject: Cost
questions.q: Explicit costs differ from implicit costs in that explicit costs:
questions.e: Explicit = out-of-pocket payments; implicit = opportunity costs of owner-supplied resources. Economic profit = revenue minus both; accounting profit deducts only explicit costs.

questions.subject: Cost
questions.q: Normal profit is:
o: The minimum return keeping an entrepreneur in the business (part of implicit cost)
questions.e: Normal profit is the opportunity cost of entrepreneurship -- included in total cost, so 'zero economic profit' still means the entrepreneur is adequately compensated.

questions.subject: Cost
questions.q: In the long run, all costs are:
questions.e: With no fixed factors long-run, every cost is variable and avoidable; the firm chooses its scale. Sunk costs, once incurred, are irrelevant to decisions.

questions.subject: Monopoly
questions.q: Marginal cost pricing (P = MC) by a monopolist would:
o: Cause losses if there are large fixed costs (natural monopoly)
questions.e: With falling AC (natural monopoly), P = MC lies below AC, causing losses -- hence regulated pricing (average-cost pricing) or subsidies are used.

questions.subject: Monopoly
questions.q: Dumping refers to:
o: Selling abroad at a lower price than at home (international price discrimination)
questions.e: Dumping = international price discrimination, often predatory; trading partners may levy anti-dumping duties.

questions.subject: Market structures compared
questions.q: A monopsony is a market with:
questions.e: Monopsony (e.g., a single large employer in a town) lets the buyer depress input prices below competitive levels.

questions.subject: Market structures compared
questions.q: Contestable markets theory says even a monopolist may price competitively if:
o: Entry and exit are costless (no sunk costs)
questions.e: Baumol's contestable markets: the threat of hit-and-run entry disciplines incumbents when sunk costs are zero.

questions.subject: Oligopoly
questions.q: The kinked demand curve's MR curve has:
o: A vertical gap at the kink
questions.e: The abrupt slope change at the kink creates a discontinuous MR with a vertical gap; MC can fluctuate within the gap without changing the profit-maximising price.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: A partner withdraws Rs. 12,000 at the beginning of every quarter. Interest on drawings is 12% p.a. The interest for the year is:
questions.e: Total drawings = Rs. 48,000. Beginning-of-quarter drawings use average 7.5 months: 48,000 x 12% x 7.5/12 = Rs. 3,600. (Middle: 6 months; end: 4.5 months.)

questions.subject: LLP Act
questions.q: In the absence of an LLP agreement, profits of an LLP are shared:
o: In the ratio of work done
questions.e: Schedule I of the LLP Act, 2008: absent agreement, partners share equally in capital, profits and losses, and have equal management rights. Partners may override this by agreement.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: An offer made to the public at large (e.g., a reward notice) is called:
questions.e: A general offer is made to the world at large and can be accepted by anyone fulfilling its terms. A specific offer is addressed to a definite person; a standing offer invites future orders.

questions.subject: Dispersion
questions.q: If mean = 20 and standard deviation = 4, the coefficient of variation is:
questions.e: CV = (4/20) x 100 = 20%. CV compares relative variability free of measurement units.

questions.subject: Dispersion
questions.q: If Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 40, the quartile deviation is:

questions.subject: Correlation
questions.q: The correlation between X and -X is:
questions.e: Y = -X is a perfect negative linear relation, so r = -1.

questions.subject: Business cycles
questions.q: Disguised unemployment, common in Indian agriculture, means:
o: More workers engaged than needed, with zero marginal productivity
questions.e: In disguised unemployment, surplus labour can be withdrawn without reducing output (MP ~ 0) -- a classic feature of traditional agriculture and the informal sector.

questions.subject: Business cycles
questions.q: The Phillips curve shows the trade-off between:
questions.e: The short-run Phillips curve: lower unemployment comes with higher inflation (and vice versa), constraining demand-management policy. Expectations can shift it.

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: Under the Companies Act, 2013, the quorum for a private company's general meeting is:
questions.e: Section 103: 2 members personally present for a private company (5/15/30 for public companies by membership size), unless the articles require more.

questions.subject: Depreciation
questions.q: A change from the WDV to the SLM depreciation method requires disclosure of:
o: The effect of the change if material, as a change in accounting estimate
questions.e: AS-6 treats a depreciation-method change as a change in estimate: applied prospectively, with disclosure of the nature and material effect of the change.

questions.subject: Inventories (AS-2)
questions.q: For measuring inventories at the year-end, AS-2 prescribes:
o: Lower of cost and net realizable value
questions.e: AS-2 requires inventories to be measured at the lower of cost and net realizable value. Cost is determined on FIFO or weighted average basis, and the comparison is made item by item (or by groups of similar items).

questions.subject: Inventories (AS-2)
questions.q: Which of the following costs is EXCLUDED from the cost of inventories under AS-2?
o: Abnormal wastage of materials, labour and other production costs
Normal freight inward on raw materials
Factory overheads based on normal capacity
questions.e: AS-2 excludes abnormal wastage, storage costs (unless necessary in the production process), administrative overheads that do not contribute to bringing inventories to their present location and condition, and selling and distribution costs from the cost of inventories.

questions.subject: Inventories (AS-2)
questions.q: Under AS-2, when raw material prices fall but the finished product's net realizable value is still above its cost, the raw materials are valued at:
o: Lower of cost and replacement cost
questions.e: Materials held for use in production are not written down below cost if the finished products in which they will be incorporated are expected to be sold at or above cost. The fall in material prices alone does not trigger a write-down in that case.

questions.subject: Events after BS date (AS-4)
questions.q: Under the revised AS-4, a dividend proposed after the balance sheet date is:
o: Not recognized as a liability; disclosed as a non-adjusting event
Recognized as a current liability at the balance sheet date
Adjusted in the financial statements of the reporting period
questions.e: Revised AS-4 treats dividends declared after the balance sheet date as non-adjusting events. No liability is recognized at the balance sheet date; the proposed dividend is disclosed in the notes in the manner required by the standard.

questions.subject: Events after BS date (AS-4)
questions.q: Which of the following is an ADJUSTING event under AS-4?
o: A decline in the market value of investments after the balance sheet date
Settlement of litigation confirming an obligation existing at the balance sheet date
A major fire destroying a plant after the balance sheet date
Announcement of a plan to discontinue an operation after the year-end
questions.e: Adjusting events provide evidence of conditions existing at the balance sheet date — e.g. settlement of litigation confirming that the enterprise already had a present obligation. Fire, discontinuation plans and post-year-end market declines reflect conditions arising after the date and are non-adjusting (disclosed only).

questions.subject: Events after BS date (AS-4)
questions.q: AS-4 requires disclosure of non-adjusting events when non-disclosure would affect users' ability to make proper evaluations. Which disclosure is NOT required for such events?
o: Updating disclosures given about conditions at the balance sheet date only if the new information affects them
Adjusting the asset and liability amounts in the balance sheet
An estimate of its financial effect, or a statement that it cannot be made
questions.e: For non-adjusting events, AS-4 requires disclosure of the nature of the event and an estimate of its financial effect (or a statement that one cannot be made). The balance sheet amounts themselves are not adjusted for events arising after the balance sheet date.

questions.subject: Government grants (AS-12)
questions.q: Under AS-12, a government grant related to a specific depreciable fixed asset should be:
o: Added to the cost of the asset
Presented as deferred income and recognized in profit and loss over the asset's useful life, or deducted from the asset's cost
Recognized as income in full in the year of receipt
questions.e: AS-12 permits two presentations for grants related to specific fixed assets: (a) show the grant as deferred income and recognize it systematically over the useful life in proportion to depreciation, or (b) deduct the grant from the gross value of the asset to arrive at book value.

questions.subject: Government grants (AS-12)
questions.q: A government grant related to revenue is received as compensation for expenses already incurred. Under AS-12 it is:
o: Deducted from the related expense in the next year
Recognized as income in the period in which it becomes receivable
Deferred and amortized over five years
questions.e: Grants related to revenue that are receivable as compensation for expenses already incurred, or for immediate financial support with no future related costs, are recognized as income in the period in which they become receivable.

questions.subject: Government grants (AS-12)
questions.q: Under AS-12, when a government grant becomes refundable, it is treated as:
questions.e: AS-12 states that a government grant that becomes refundable is treated as an extraordinary item. The amount refundable is first applied against any unamortized deferred credit relating to the grant; the balance is charged to profit and loss.

questions.subject: Investments (AS-13)
questions.q: Under AS-13, current investments are carried in the financial statements at:
o: Higher of cost and fair value
Lower of cost and fair value, determined either on an individual investment basis or by category
questions.e: AS-13 requires current investments to be carried at the lower of cost and fair value. The comparison may be done for each investment individually or for each category of investment, but not on an aggregate portfolio basis across categories.

questions.subject: Investments (AS-13)
questions.q: Under AS-13, a long-term investment that suffers a decline in value which is OTHER than temporary is:
o: Written down to recognize the decline; the reduction is charged to profit and loss
Kept at cost with no adjustment
questions.e: Long-term investments are carried at cost, but when there is a decline, other than temporary, in their value, the carrying amount is reduced to recognize the decline and the reduction is charged to the statement of profit and loss.

questions.subject: Investments (AS-13)
questions.q: Under AS-13, on disposal of part of a holding of an investment, the cost to be matched against proceeds is determined on:
o: Average carrying amount of the total holding
questions.e: AS-13 states that on disposal of a part of the holding of an individual investment, the carrying amount allocated to the portion sold is determined on the basis of the average carrying amount of the total holding of the investment.

questions.subject: Borrowing costs (AS-16)
questions.q: Under AS-16, borrowing costs directly attributable to the acquisition of a qualifying asset must be:
o: Deferred and written off over the loan period
Capitalized as part of the cost of the asset
questions.e: AS-16 requires borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset to be capitalized as part of that asset's cost. A qualifying asset is one that necessarily takes a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale.

questions.subject: Borrowing costs (AS-16)
questions.q: Under AS-16, capitalization of borrowing costs is SUSPENDED during:
o: Periods when the enterprise earns interest on surplus borrowed funds
The period before any expenditure on the asset is incurred
Extended periods in which active development of the qualifying asset is interrupted
Normal temporary delays inherent in the construction process
questions.e: Capitalization is suspended during extended periods when active development is interrupted (e.g. work stoppages). Temporary, normal delays that are a necessary part of the process (like high-water periods for a bridge) do not suspend capitalization.

questions.subject: Borrowing costs (AS-16)
questions.q: Under AS-16, income earned on the temporary investment of specific borrowings pending their expenditure on a qualifying asset is:
o: Added to the cost of the qualifying asset
Deducted from the borrowing costs eligible for capitalization
Recognized as other income with no adjustment
questions.e: When funds are borrowed specifically for a qualifying asset, the borrowing costs eligible for capitalization are reduced by any investment income earned on the temporary investment of those borrowings before they are spent on the asset.

questions.subject: Segment reporting (AS-17)
questions.q: Under AS-17, a business or geographical segment is identified as a REPORTABLE segment if its revenue is:
o: 10% or more of the total revenue of all segments
questions.e: AS-17's 10% thresholds apply to revenue, result and assets: a segment is reportable if its revenue (internal + external) is 10% or more of total segment revenue, its result is 10% or more of the combined result, or its assets are 10% or more of total segment assets.

questions.subject: Segment reporting (AS-17)
questions.q: AS-17 requires that if the total EXTERNAL revenue of reportable segments is less than 75% of enterprise revenue, the enterprise should:
o: Identify additional segments as reportable even if they do not meet the 10% thresholds
Stop segment reporting for the year
questions.e: The 75% test ensures most of the enterprise's revenue is covered by segment reporting. If reportable segments' external revenue falls below 75% of total enterprise revenue, additional segments must be designated as reportable until the threshold is met.

questions.subject: Segment reporting (AS-17)
questions.q: Under AS-17, a business segment is distinguished from other segments primarily on the basis of:
o: The legal structure of the enterprise
Risks and returns associated with its products or services
questions.e: A business segment is a distinguishable component engaged in providing products or services subject to risks and returns different from those of other business segments. Dominant source of risks and returns decides whether business or geographical segments are primary.

questions.subject: Related parties (AS-18)
questions.q: Under AS-18, which of the following is treated as a related party?
o: A major customer with no ownership or control link
A trade union of the enterprise's employees
A government department regulating the industry
Key management personnel of the reporting enterprise
questions.e: AS-18 related parties include holding/subsidiary/associate companies, key management personnel, relatives of KMP, and enterprises over which KMP or their relatives exercise significant influence. Ordinary customers, unions and regulators without control or significant influence are not related parties.

questions.subject: Related parties (AS-18)
questions.q: AS-18 requires disclosure of:
o: Only the names of all related parties without transaction details
Transactions with related parties only if they are at arm's length
Related party relationships only when control exists
The name of the transacting related party, the nature of the relationship, and the nature and volume of transactions
questions.e: AS-18 mandates disclosure of the related party relationship (name and nature), a description of transactions between the parties, and the volumes involved (amounts, outstanding balances). Arm's length assertions need not be disclosed unless they can be substantiated.

questions.subject: Related parties (AS-18)
questions.q: Under AS-18, 'significant influence' over an enterprise is generally presumed when the investor holds:
o: 10% or more of the voting power
Any holding with a board seat
20% or more of the voting power
questions.e: AS-18 presumes significant influence when an enterprise holds, directly or indirectly, 20% or more of the voting power of another enterprise — the same threshold used for associates under AS-23.

questions.subject: Leases (AS-19)
questions.q: Under AS-19, a lease is classified as a FINANCE lease when it:
o: Covers more than 75% of the asset's useful life
Contains a bargain purchase option only
Transfers substantially all the risks and rewards incidental to ownership to the lessee
questions.e: AS-19 classifies leases by substance: a finance lease transfers substantially all risks and rewards of ownership (e.g. ownership transfers at end, bargain purchase option, lease term covers major part of life, PV of payments covers substantially all fair value). All other leases are operating leases.

questions.subject: Leases (AS-19)
questions.q: Under AS-19, at the inception of a finance lease, the lessee recognizes the asset and liability at:
o: The higher of fair value and present value of minimum lease payments
The total of all lease rentals payable
The written-down value in the lessor's books
The lower of the fair value of the leased asset and the present value of minimum lease payments
questions.e: The lessee records a finance lease at an amount equal to the fair value of the leased asset or, if lower, the present value of the minimum lease payments at inception, each determined at the lease's inception.

questions.subject: Leases (AS-19)
questions.q: Under AS-19, lease payments under an OPERATING lease are recognized by the lessee as:
o: A reduction of a lease liability
An expense on a straight-line basis over the lease term
questions.e: Operating lease payments are recognized as an expense in the statement of profit and loss on a straight-line basis over the lease term (unless another systematic basis is more representative of the time pattern of benefit).

questions.subject: Taxes on income (AS-22)
questions.q: Under AS-22, deferred tax arises on account of:
o: Permanent differences between tax and accounting income
Differences in accounting policies between group companies
Errors in prior period tax computations
Timing differences between taxable income and accounting income
questions.e: AS-22 deals only with timing differences — differences between taxable income and accounting income that originate in one period and reverse in later periods (e.g. different depreciation rates). Permanent differences (like exempt income) never reverse and create no deferred tax.

questions.subject: Taxes on income (AS-22)
questions.q: Under AS-22, a deferred tax ASSET should be recognized:
o: In all cases where timing differences exist
Only for carry-forward losses, never for other timing differences
At the enacted future tax rate expected ten years ahead
Only when there is reasonable certainty of sufficient future taxable income against which it can be realized
questions.e: Deferred tax assets are recognized only to the extent there is reasonable certainty of realization. Where there are unabsorbed depreciation or carried-forward losses, recognition requires virtual certainty supported by convincing evidence.

questions.subject: Taxes on income (AS-22)
questions.q: Under AS-22, the tax expense for the period comprises:
o: Current tax minus MAT credit always
questions.e: Tax expense = current tax (tax payable on taxable income for the period) + deferred tax (tax effect of timing differences). Both components are presented in the statement of profit and loss.

questions.subject: Intangibles (AS-26)
questions.q: Under AS-26, expenditure on RESEARCH should be:
o: Recognized as an expense in the period incurred
Deferred over the project's expected life
questions.e: AS-26 draws a sharp line: research costs are always expensed when incurred. Development costs may be capitalized only if technical feasibility, intent and ability to complete, and probable future economic benefits are demonstrated.

questions.subject: Intangibles (AS-26)
questions.q: Under AS-26, the amortization period of an intangible asset is based on the best estimate of useful life, subject to a rebuttable presumption that it will not exceed:
o: Ten years from the date the asset is available for use
The legal life of the right
questions.e: AS-26 presumes the useful life of an intangible will not exceed ten years from availability for use. The presumption can be rebutted only with persuasive evidence (e.g. a longer contractual or legal right).

questions.subject: Provisions (AS-29)
questions.q: Under AS-29, a provision is recognized when:
o: There is a present obligation from a past event, a probable outflow of resources, and a reliable estimate can be made
Management intends to incur expenditure in future
There is a possible obligation whose existence is uncertain
The board has approved a budget for the item
questions.e: AS-29's three recognition conditions: a present obligation (legal or constructive) arising from a past event, probable outflow of economic benefits, and a reliable estimate. Future intentions or mere possibilities do not qualify.

questions.subject: Provisions (AS-29)
questions.q: Under AS-29, a CONTINGENT liability is:
o: Disclosed in the notes unless the possibility of outflow is remote
Recognized when the outflow is merely possible
questions.e: Contingent liabilities are not recognized in the balance sheet. They are disclosed in the notes unless the possibility of an outflow is remote, in which case even disclosure is not required.

questions.subject: EPS (AS-20)
questions.q: Basic EPS under AS-20 is computed as:
o: Net profit attributable to equity shareholders divided by the weighted average number of equity shares outstanding
Profit after tax divided by shares at year-end
Operating profit divided by weighted average shares
Net profit before preference dividend divided by equity shares
questions.e: Basic EPS = net profit or loss for the period attributable to equity shareholders (after preference dividends) / weighted average number of equity shares outstanding during the period.

questions.subject: EPS (AS-20)
questions.q: Under AS-20, when a bonus issue is made during the year, the weighted average shares for prior periods presented are:
o: Restated as if the bonus shares had always been outstanding
Adjusted only for the current year
questions.e: Bonus issues, share splits and consolidations involve no consideration, so AS-20 requires restating the number of shares for all prior periods presented as if the event had occurred at the beginning of the earliest period reported.

questions.subject: Accounting concepts & standards
questions.q: Capital contributed by the proprietor is shown as a liability of the business because of the:
questions.e: The business entity concept treats the business as separate from its owners, so the proprietor's capital is shown as a liability of the business owed to the owner.

questions.subject: Accounting concepts & standards
questions.q: Under the realisation concept, revenue from sale of goods is recognized:
o: When the sales order is received
When the goods are sold and ownership passes to the buyer
When the quotation is sent to the customer
questions.e: The realisation (revenue recognition) concept requires revenue to be recognized only when it is reasonably certain — normally at the point of sale when ownership and risks pass to the buyer, not when the order is received or goods are manufactured.

questions.subject: Accounting concepts & standards
questions.q: Under the concept of materiality, whether an item is material depends on:
o: Its nature or size relative to the enterprise
questions.e: Materiality means an item is material if its omission or misstatement could influence users' decisions. A Rs. 500 calculator for a large company is immaterial and may be expensed immediately, while the same item could be material for a tiny firm.

questions.subject: Accounting concepts & standards
questions.q: AS-1 builds accounting policies on certain fundamental assumptions. Which trio does the standard name as fundamental?
questions.e: AS-1 names going concern, consistency and accrual as the fundamental accounting assumptions. If these are followed, no disclosure is needed; if any is not followed, the fact must be disclosed.

questions.subject: Bank reconciliation
questions.q: Cash book shows a debit balance of Rs. 25,000. A customer directly deposited Rs. 4,000 into the bank (not recorded in cash book) and the bank charged Rs. 500 as commission. What is the pass book balance?
questions.e: In a BRS prepared from the cash book, add items appearing only in the pass book that increase the balance (direct deposits, interest credited) and deduct items appearing only in the pass book that reduce it (bank charges, standing instructions). A cheque issued but not presented is deducted from the cash book balance? Let's work: cash book debit balance 25,000; add direct deposit 4,000; less bank charges 500 = 28,500.

questions.subject: Bank reconciliation
questions.q: Pass book shows a credit balance of Rs. 18,000. Cheques deposited Rs. 3,000 were not yet cleared, and cheques issued Rs. 2,000 were not yet presented. What is the cash book balance?
questions.e: A cheque deposited but not yet cleared appears as a debit in the cash book but not in the pass book. Starting from the pass book balance, add it (and other cash-book-only debits) to reach the cash book balance: 18,000 + 3,000 - 2,000 (unpresented cheques) = 19,000.

questions.subject: Bank reconciliation
questions.q: Cash book shows a credit balance (overdraft) of Rs. 10,000. Bank debited Rs. 1,000 as interest on overdraft and collected Rs. 5,000 directly from a debtor (not recorded). The pass book will show:
questions.e: An overdraft means the cash book has a credit balance — money owed to the bank. Starting from the credit balance of Rs. 10,000, add bank interest debited Rs. 1,000 (increases overdraft) and deduct the direct collection Rs. 5,000: 10,000 + 1,000 - 5,000 = Rs. 6,000 credit balance in the cash book corresponds to Rs. 6,000 overdraft in the pass book.

questions.subject: Bank reconciliation
questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a reconciling item in a Bank Reconciliation Statement?
o: Errors in casting the cash book
Identical entries correctly recorded in both books on the same date
questions.e: BRS timing differences arise because the cash book and pass book are written up at different times (unpresented cheques, uncleared deposits, direct debits/credits). Posting errors and omissions cause differences too, but a BRS is specifically the reconciliation statement — the question asks which is NOT a valid reconciling item: a correctly recorded identical entry in both books needs no reconciliation.

questions.subject: Joint venture
questions.q: In a joint venture recorded by the memorandum method:
o: Each co-venturer records only his own transactions in a personal account with the other co-venturer
A separate set of books is always maintained
All transactions are recorded in the books of one co-venturer only
The venture is treated as a partnership firm
questions.e: Under the memorandum joint venture method, each co-venturer records only his own transactions with the joint venture in a personal 'Joint Venture with ...' account; no separate joint venture account is maintained in the books — the memorandum account shows each party's contribution.

questions.subject: Joint venture
questions.q: When separate books are kept for a joint venture, the account that collects all venture transactions is the:
questions.e: When separate books are maintained for the joint venture, it is treated like a temporary partnership: a Joint Venture Account is debited with purchases and expenses and credited with sales, and the profit or loss is shared in the agreed ratio.

questions.subject: Joint venture
questions.q: In a joint venture, unsold stock costing Rs. 25,000 is taken over by co-venturer A at an agreed value of Rs. 30,000. The entry in the joint venture books is:
o: Debited to Joint Venture Account with Rs. 30,000
Debited to Purchases Account with Rs. 30,000
Credited to Joint Venture Account with Rs. 30,000
Credited to Stock Account with Rs. 25,000
questions.e: Stock taken over by a co-venturer at an agreed valuation is credited to the Joint Venture Account (reducing the cost) and debited to the co-venturer's personal account. Here the JV account is credited with Rs. 30,000.

questions.subject: Joint venture
questions.q: A co-venturer is entitled to 5% commission on venture sales of Rs. 2,00,000. The correct entry is:
o: Debit Co-venturer's account, credit Joint Venture Account
Debit Joint Venture Account, credit Bank
Debit Joint Venture Account, credit Co-venturer's personal account
questions.e: Commission on sales is a venture expense: debit Joint Venture Account, credit the co-venturer entitled to the commission (or his personal account). Expenses of the venture always go to the debit of the Joint Venture Account.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: A, B and C share profits 1/2 : 1/3 : 1/6. A retires and B and C agree to share future profits 2:1. The gaining ratio of B and C is:
questions.e: Gaining ratio = new profit-sharing ratio minus old ratio. B: 1/3 - 1/4 = 4/12 - 3/12 = 1/12; C: 1/2 - 1/2 = 0? Wait: old ratios A:B:C = 3:2:1? Let's recompute: A:B:C = 1/2:1/3:1/6. After A retires, B:C = 2:1. B's gain = 2/3 - 1/3 = 1/3; C's gain = 1/3 - 1/6 = 1/6. Gaining ratio B:C = 1/3 : 1/6 = 2:1.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: A retires from a firm (old ratio A:B:C = 5:3:2). B and C continue sharing 3:2. Goodwill is valued at Rs. 60,000 (not to appear in books). The adjustment entry debits:
o: Rs. 30,000 to B and Rs. 30,000 to C
Rs. 36,000 to B and Rs. 24,000 to C
Rs. 24,000 to B and Rs. 36,000 to C
Rs. 20,000 each to A, B and C
questions.e: On retirement, the retiring partner's share of goodwill is credited to his capital account and debited to the continuing partners' capital accounts in their gaining ratio. B's gain = 3/5-1/2 = 1/10, C's gain = 2/5-1/2 = -1/10? Hmm: old A:B:C = 5:3:2? Let's take old 5:3:2, new B:C = 3:2. B gain = 3/5 - 3/10 = 3/10; C gain = 2/5 - 2/10 = 2/10 = 1/5. Ratio 3:2. Goodwill Rs. 60,000: B debited 36,000, C debited 24,000.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: Under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, a retiring partner's liability to third parties:
o: He is discharged from all past and future liabilities automatically
His liability ends only after the final settlement is paid
He remains liable for acts done before retirement unless released by agreement with the third party
He is liable only if the firm continues to use the old firm name
questions.e: The retiring partner remains liable for acts done before retirement. Public notice of retirement (Sec 32) discharges liability for acts done after retirement; without notice, liability to third parties continues.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: On the death of a partner, the treatment of profit up to the date of death is:
o: No profit is credited after the last balance sheet date
Profit is credited only if the partnership deed expressly provides
Interest on capital continues till the executor is paid
The deceased partner's estimated share of profit up to the date of death is credited to his account
questions.e: The deceased partner's share of profit up to the date of death is estimated (by time or turnover basis if the deed is silent) and credited to his capital/executor's account. Interest on capital stops at death; drawings after death don't apply; the executor doesn't automatically become a partner.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: The legal representative (executor) of a deceased partner is entitled to:
o: The deceased partner's capital, goodwill share and profits up to death
A right to become a partner in place of the deceased
Interest on the balance due at the firm's borrowing rate automatically
A share in profits earned after the date of death
questions.e: The executor of a deceased partner is entitled to the deceased's capital, share of goodwill, reserves, and profits up to death (less drawings). The executor cannot claim to become a partner or demand dissolution unless the deed or agreement provides so.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: Under Section 37 of the Partnership Act, if the firm continues using a deceased partner's unpaid balance, his estate may claim:
o: Only the balance standing to his credit
Interest at 6% p.a. or the share of profits attributable to the unpaid amount, at the outgoing partner's option
Double the market rate of interest
questions.e: Section 37: where the surviving partners continue the business with the deceased/retired partner's money unpaid, the outgoing partner (or his estate) can claim either interest at 6% p.a. or the share of profits attributable to his unpaid amount — at his option.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: A firm's last four years' profits: Rs. 80,000, Rs. 90,000, Rs. 70,000, Rs. 1,00,000. Normal profit on capital employed is Rs. 60,000 p.a. Goodwill at 3 years' purchase of super profits is:

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: Capital employed Rs. 5,00,000, 10% debentures Rs. 1,00,000, non-trade investments Rs. 50,000. Normal rate of return 10%. Average maintainable profit Rs. 70,000. Goodwill at 2 years' purchase of super profits:
questions.e: Capital employed = 5,00,000 + 1,00,000 - 50,000 = 5,50,000. Normal profit = 5,50,000 x 10% = 55,000. Average profit = 70,000. Super profit = 15,000. Goodwill = 15,000 x 2 = Rs. 30,000.

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: Super profit Rs. 40,000 p.a. Goodwill by the annuity method (3 years, 10% p.a., annuity factor 2.4869) is:
questions.e: Under the annuity/capitalization method, goodwill = super profit x annuity factor. Annuity of Re. 1 for 3 years at 10% = [1 - (1.1)^-3]/0.10 = 2.4869. Goodwill = 40,000 x 2.4869 = Rs. 99,476 (approx Rs. 99,480).

questions.subject: Partnership
questions.q: X is guaranteed a minimum profit of Rs. 24,000 by partners Y and Z (profit ratio X:Y:Z = 1:3:1). Firm profit is Rs. 1,00,000. The shortfall is borne by:
o: Y bears Rs. 3,000 and Z bears Rs. 1,000
The firm absorbs Rs. 4,000 as a loss
X gets only Rs. 20,000 with no make-up
questions.e: A guarantee of minimum profit means the firm (or guaranteeing partners) makes good any shortfall below the guaranteed amount. X's share = 1,00,000 x 1/5 = 20,000; shortfall = 24,000 - 20,000 = 4,000 borne by Y and Z in 3:1 = 3,000 and 1,000.

questions.subject: Partnership accounts
questions.q: Regarding interest on partners' capital:
o: It is payable even out of capital
It is always 6% p.a. by statute
It is payable only if the deed provides, and only out of profits
It is charged at the bank rate
questions.e: Interest on capital is payable only if the partnership deed provides for it, and then only out of profits (unless the deed says otherwise). If profits are insufficient, interest is restricted to available profits and shared in the interest ratio.

questions.subject: Partnership accounts
questions.q: Under the fluctuating capital method:
o: Drawings are credited to capital accounts
Interest on drawings is credited to capital
Current accounts must still be maintained
All adjustments including profit share go directly to the capital accounts
questions.e: When capitals are fluctuating, all adjustments (interest, salary, drawings, profit share) go directly to the capital accounts and no current accounts are maintained. Fixed capitals use separate current accounts.

questions.subject: Rectification of errors
questions.q: Machinery purchased for Rs. 50,000 was debited to Purchases Account. The rectifying entry is:
o: Debit Machinery Account, credit Purchases Account
Debit Purchases Account, credit Machinery Account
Debit Suspense Account, credit Machinery Account
No entry is needed as the trial balance agrees
questions.e: A purchase of machinery debited to Purchases is an error of principle. The rectifying entry debits Machinery and credits Purchases (or the Suspense-corrected route): correct the classification — Debit Machinery Account, Credit Purchases Account.

questions.subject: Rectification of errors
questions.q: Rs. 2,000 received from Ram was credited to Shyam's account. The rectifying entry is:
o: Debit Shyam's Account, credit Ram's Account
questions.e: Rs. 2,000 received from Ram credited to Shyam is an error of commission. Rectify by debiting Shyam's account (removing the wrong credit) and crediting Ram's account.

questions.subject: Rectification of errors
questions.q: A Suspense Account is opened to hold the difference arising from:
o: Errors affecting only one side of an account
questions.e: One-sided errors (e.g. wrong casting of a subsidiary book, omission of posting to one account) throw the trial balance out of agreement, and the difference is parked in a Suspense Account until detected. Two-sided errors keep the trial balance agreeing.

questions.subject: Rectification of errors
questions.q: A credit purchase of Rs. 9,000 was recorded as Rs. 900 in the purchases book and the supplier's account. The correct treatment is:
o: It is an error of principle
Debit Purchases Rs. 8,100, credit Supplier Rs. 8,100; no suspense needed
questions.e: A credit purchase of Rs. 9,000 recorded as Rs. 900 in both the purchase book and the supplier's account is an error of original entry affecting both sides equally — the trial balance still agrees, so no suspense account is involved. Rectify by debiting Purchases 8,100 and crediting the Supplier 8,100.

questions.subject: Cash flow basics
questions.q: Under AS-3, which of the following is a cash flow from OPERATING activities?
questions.e: Operating activities = principal revenue-producing activities: cash from customers, paid to suppliers/employees, taxes on income. Purchase of machinery is investing; dividend paid is financing; issue of shares is financing.

questions.subject: Cash flow basics
questions.q: Using the indirect method under AS-3, operating cash flow is derived by:
o: Profit before tax Rs. 2,00,000; add depreciation Rs. 30,000; less increase in inventory Rs. 20,000
Profit before tax Rs. 2,00,000; less depreciation Rs. 30,000; add increase in inventory Rs. 20,000
Net profit Rs. 2,00,000; add increase in debtors Rs. 20,000
Cash from customers minus cash paid to suppliers only
questions.e: AS-3 permits the indirect method to start from profit/loss and adjust for non-cash items (depreciation), non-operating items (interest), and working capital changes. Increase in inventory is deducted; increase in creditors is added.

questions.subject: Cash flow basics
questions.q: For a non-financial enterprise under AS-3, which item is classified as an INVESTING cash flow?
o: Interest received on investments by a trading company
questions.e: Interest and dividends RECEIVED are investing cash flows (for non-financial enterprises). Interest paid is financing (or operating under the direct classification choice); dividends paid are financing.

questions.subject: Ratio analysis
questions.q: Current assets Rs. 3,00,000 and current liabilities Rs. 1,50,000. The current ratio is:
questions.e: Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities = 3,00,000 / 1,50,000 = 2:1. An ideal current ratio is generally considered 2:1.

questions.subject: Ratio analysis
questions.q: The debt-equity ratio is computed as ______, and a lower ratio indicates:
questions.e: Debt-equity ratio = Long-term debt / Equity (shareholders' funds). A lower ratio means less reliance on borrowed funds and lower financial risk.

questions.subject: Ratio analysis
questions.q: Cost of goods sold Rs. 6,00,000; opening inventory Rs. 1,20,000; closing inventory Rs. 1,80,000. The inventory turnover ratio is:
questions.e: Inventory turnover = Cost of goods sold / Average inventory = 6,00,000 / 1,50,000 = 4 times. A higher ratio generally indicates efficient inventory management.

questions.subject: Trial balance & errors
questions.q: A sale of Rs. 4,500 was recorded in the sales book as Rs. 5,400. The trial balance will:
o: It will not agree; debtors are overstated
It will agree because both debit and credit carry the same wrong figure
It will agree only after a suspense entry
It will disagree by Rs. 900 on the credit side
questions.e: Sales recorded in the sales book as Rs. 5,400 instead of Rs. 4,500 is an error of commission (wrong amount in original entry) affecting both debit (debtor) and credit (sales) equally, so the trial balance still agrees.

questions.subject: Rectification of errors
questions.q: A trial balance shows total debits of ₹4,58,200 and total credits of ₹4,55,900. To make the totals agree temporarily, the ₹2,300 difference is:
o: Written off to the profit and loss account
questions.e: The credit column is short by ₹2,300 (4,58,200 − 4,55,900), so the suspense account is credited with ₹2,300 and entered in the credit column to make the two sides agree. When the one-sided error is later located and rectified, the suspense account is closed; no permanent entry is made to capital or to profit and loss.

questions.subject: Capital vs revenue
questions.q: Which of the following is a REVENUE expenditure?
questions.e: Revenue expenditure benefits only the current period (repairs, salaries, rent). Capital expenditure creates or improves a long-term asset (purchase of machinery, major overhauls extending life).

questions.subject: Capital vs revenue
questions.q: Heavy advertising expenditure on launching a new product, treated as deferred revenue expenditure, is:
o: It is shown permanently as an asset
It is written off over the periods it benefits
It is added to share capital
It is treated as a contingent liability
questions.e: Deferred revenue expenditure (e.g. heavy advertisement for a new product launch) benefits more than one period but is not a tangible asset; it is written off over the periods benefited, typically 3-5 years.

questions.subject: Provisions
questions.q: A provision for doubtful debts is:
o: A charge against profits for a known liability of uncertain amount
questions.e: A provision is a present obligation of uncertain timing or amount (e.g. provision for doubtful debts, provision for taxation) and is charged to profit and loss. A reserve is an appropriation of profit, not a charge.

questions.subject: Average due date
questions.q: Three bills due 31-1-2026 (Rs. 10,000), 2-3-2026 (Rs. 20,000) and 1-4-2026 (Rs. 30,000) are replaced by a single payment. Taking 1-1-2026 as the base date, the average due date is:
questions.e: Average due date = base date + (sum of products / sum of amounts). Products: 10,000x30 + 20,000x60 + 30,000x90 = 3,00,000 + 12,00,000 + 27,00,000 = 42,00,000. Total = 60,000. Average period = 70 days. Base date 1 Jan + 70 days = 12 March 2026 (Jan has 31 days: 30 days to 31 Jan, 40 more days in Feb = 28 days in 2026, leaving 12 days into March).

questions.subject: Average due date
questions.q: The average due date method is applied when:
o: Several amounts due on different dates are settled by one payment without interest loss to either party
questions.e: Average due date is used when one party owes several amounts due on different dates to the other (or vice versa) and they agree to settle with a single payment without loss of interest to either side.

questions.subject: Account current
questions.q: In an Account Current prepared by the product method, interest is calculated:
o: On each item from its due date to the closing date, using the product method
At a flat rate on the closing balance
questions.e: In an account current, interest is calculated on each transaction from its due date to the closing date using the product method; the net interest (balance of products x rate/365) is entered on the side with the larger product total.

questions.subject: Account current
questions.q: Three days of grace are NOT allowed for:
questions.e: Days of grace (3 days) apply to bills of exchange and promissory notes payable after date or after sight, but NOT to instruments payable on demand, and an account current balance payable on a fixed date is not a negotiable instrument at all.

questions.subject: Incomplete records
questions.q: Opening debtors Rs. 40,000, closing debtors Rs. 60,000, cash received from debtors Rs. 2,40,000. Credit sales for the year are:
questions.e: Under single entry, credit sales = closing debtors + cash received from debtors - opening debtors = 60,000 + 2,40,000 - 40,000 = Rs. 2,60,000.

questions.subject: Incomplete records
questions.q: Opening creditors Rs. 30,000, closing creditors Rs. 50,000, cash paid to creditors Rs. 1,80,000. Credit purchases are:
questions.e: Credit purchases = closing creditors + payments to creditors - opening creditors = 50,000 + 1,80,000 - 30,000 = Rs. 2,00,000.

questions.subject: Fixed assets
questions.q: Under AS-10, a self-constructed fixed asset is recorded at:
o: Direct cost plus attributable overheads, excluding internal profits
questions.e: AS-10 requires self-constructed assets to be capitalized at cost, which includes direct materials, direct labour, and directly attributable overheads — the same cost elements as a purchased asset, excluding internal profits and abnormal costs.

questions.subject: Fixed assets
questions.q: Under AS-10, subsequent expenditure on a fixed asset after its acquisition is capitalized when:
o: It is capitalized only if it improves the asset beyond its originally assessed performance
It is debited to a revaluation reserve
questions.e: Subsequent expenditure is capitalized only if it increases future benefits beyond the previously assessed standard of performance (e.g. an upgrade raising capacity). Routine repairs maintaining existing performance are expensed.

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: The maximum capital a company is authorized to raise, as stated in its Memorandum of Association, is:
questions.e: Authorized (nominal/registered) capital is the maximum amount stated in the Memorandum of Association that the company may raise. Issued capital is the portion offered; subscribed is the portion taken up.

questions.subject: Company accounts
questions.q: Preliminary expenses of a company are:
o: Written off against securities premium first, then against profits
Always carried forward as a fictitious asset
Added to the cost of fixed assets
questions.e: Preliminary (formation) expenses are written off first against the Securities Premium Account if available, and any balance against profits over a reasonable period — they are never carried as a fictitious asset indefinitely.

questions.subject: Amalgamation concepts
questions.q: Under the pooling of interests method for amalgamation in the nature of merger:
o: At fair values with goodwill recognized
At their existing book values, preserving the identity of reserves
questions.e: In an amalgamation in the nature of merger (pooling of interests), assets, liabilities and reserves of the transferor are recorded at their existing book values, and the identity of reserves is preserved.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: A 'contingent contract' is defined under which section of the Indian Contract Act, 1872?
questions.e: Section 31 defines a contingent contract as one to do or not to do something if some event, collateral to the contract, does or does not happen. Insurance and indemnity contracts are classic examples.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Under Section 32, a contingent contract dependent on the happening of an uncertain future event:
o: It can be enforced only after the event happens
The promisor must perform within a reasonable time
It is treated as a wagering agreement
questions.e: Section 32: a contingent contract to do something on the happening of an uncertain future event cannot be enforced until the event happens. If the event becomes impossible, the contract becomes void.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: A contingent agreement based on the happening of an impossible event is, under Section 36:
o: Voidable at the option of the promisor
Valid if both parties were unaware
Void, whether or not the parties knew of the impossibility
questions.e: Section 36: contingent agreements to do or not to do anything if an impossible event happens are void, whether the impossibility was known or not at the time of agreement.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Under Section 73, compensation for breach of contract is available for:
o: Only loss which naturally arose in the usual course or was in the contemplation of both parties
questions.e: Section 73 embodies the rule in Hadley v Baxendale: compensation is limited to loss which naturally arose in the usual course of things, or which the parties knew was likely when the contract was made. Remote and indirect losses are excluded.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: When a contract names a sum payable on breach, Section 74 entitles the aggrieved party to:
o: Reasonable compensation not exceeding the sum named in the contract
The full sum named, without proof of loss
Nothing, as penalty clauses are void
questions.e: Section 74: where a sum is named as payable on breach (liquidated damages) or a penalty is stipulated, the aggrieved party is entitled to reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount named — proof of actual loss is not dispensed with, but the named sum caps recovery.

questions.subject: Indian Contract Act
questions.q: Under Section 75, a party who rightfully rescinds a contract:
o: He must perform his part first
He is entitled to compensation for damage from non-fulfilment
He forfeits all rights under the contract
He can claim only the contract price
questions.e: Section 75: a person who rightfully rescinds a contract is entitled to compensation for damage sustained through non-fulfilment. Rescission is available where the other party's breach goes to the root or where the contract is voidable.

questions.subject: Indian Partnership Act
questions.q: Under Section 69 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, the effect of non-registration is:
o: Third parties cannot sue an unregistered firm
Partners of an unregistered firm can sue the firm for their dues
An unregistered firm cannot enforce contractual rights by suit, though third parties may sue it
Registration is compulsory for a firm to exist
questions.e: Section 69: an unregistered firm cannot sue to enforce rights arising from a contract, and partners cannot sue the firm or each other. However, suits for dissolution, accounts of a dissolved firm, and realization of property are allowed; third parties can always sue the firm.

questions.subject: Indian Partnership Act
questions.q: Which of the following suits is NOT barred by non-registration of a firm under Section 69?
o: Suits between partners for profit shares
Suits by the firm against third parties on contracts
Suits for dissolution and accounts of a dissolved firm
questions.e: Section 69(3) and (4) preserve the right to sue for dissolution of the firm, for accounts of a dissolved firm, and for realization of the property of a dissolved firm even without registration. Criminal proceedings and statutory rights (e.g. under insolvency law) are also unaffected.

questions.subject: Indian Partnership Act
questions.q: Under Section 30 of the Partnership Act, a minor may be admitted:
o: With the consent of all partners, to the benefits of an existing partnership
As a full partner with unlimited liability
Without any consent if he contributes capital
questions.e: Section 30: a minor may be admitted to the benefits of an existing partnership with the consent of all partners. His share is liable for the firm's acts, but he is not personally liable, and he must elect within six months of attaining majority whether to become a partner.

questions.subject: Indian Partnership Act
questions.q: A minor admitted to the benefits of partnership attains majority and elects to become a partner. The consequence is:
o: His liability remains limited to his share
He becomes personally liable for all acts of the firm since he was admitted to benefits
questions.e: On attaining majority, the minor must give public notice within six months of his election to become or not become a partner. If he elects to become a partner, he becomes personally liable for all acts of the firm done since his admission to benefits.

questions.subject: Indian Partnership Act
questions.q: Under Section 25 of the Partnership Act, a partner's liability for acts of the firm is:
o: Only to the extent of his capital contribution
Only for acts he personally authorized
Jointly with all other partners and also severally
Only after the firm's assets are exhausted
questions.e: Section 25: every partner is liable jointly with all other partners and also severally for all acts of the firm done while he is a partner. A partner's private assets can therefore be reached for firm debts.

questions.subject: Indian Partnership Act
questions.q: Under Sections 26 and 27 of the Partnership Act, the firm's liability for a partner's wrongful acts is:
o: The firm is never liable for a partner's wrongs
Only the wrongdoing partner is liable
The firm is liable only if it ratified the act
The firm is liable for a partner's wrongful act or misapplication done in the ordinary course of business
questions.e: Section 26 makes the firm liable for loss caused by a partner's wrongful act or omission in the ordinary course of business or with the authority of his partners. Section 27 makes the firm liable for misapplication of money or property received by a partner within the scope of his apparent authority.

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: Under the Companies Act, 2013, a company is essentially:
o: An artificial person with separate legal existence and perpetual succession
A partnership with more than fifty members
A trust registered under the Trusts Act
questions.e: A company is an artificial person created by law with perpetual succession and a separate legal personality — it can own property, sue and be sued in its own name, and its members' liability is generally limited.

questions.subject: Companies Act
questions.q: The doctrine of lifting the corporate veil is applied by courts when:
o: The company has only two members
The corporate form is used to perpetrate fraud or evade legal obligations
